subtopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
Mr. HAZEN moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 81, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.
He said: This Bill proposes to repeal sections 442, 443 and 444 of the Canada Shipping Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, chapter 113, and to substitute two sections in lieu thereof. By the provisions of the Act, chapter 48 of the Statute of 1914, all powers with respect to pilots and apprentices, formerly vested in the Quebec Pilots Corporation, become vested in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It will therefore be seen that section 442 is no longer operative for the same reason. All the powers with respect to pilots in the Quebec district are now vested in the minister, and the only portion of section 443 as it stands at present that it is necessary to retain is the portion defining the number of pilots in the district. The effect of section 444 as it stands at present is that if the period1 of apprenticeship of an apprentice is interrupted for a longer period than four months, no matter for what cause, illness or any other cause over which the apprentice can have no control, even although the interruption may be in no way due to any fault of his own, it is not possible for the apprentice -to complete his term and obtain his license. The term of an apprentice is seven years, certain voyages and conditions being required during that period. An apprentice may be incapacitated in the sixth year of his ser-

vice for a longer period than four months, and it certainly would be an injustice for such an apprentice to be unable to complete his term of service after having served six years, if the interruption was due to a cause not his own fault. It is proposed by . the Bill under consideration to enable apprentices whose period of service may, for legitimate reasons, be interrupted, to make up for such time as has been lost, provided, of course, they, are in every other respect found suitable for appointment and that before a license is issued the full period of seven years apprenticeship has been filled.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

subtopic: CANADIAN NAVAL SERVICE.
CANADIAN NAVAL SERVICE.
speechtext:
Referring to a debate on Naval aid, which . took place oh June 6, 1913, as reported in Hansard of 1912-13, page 13142, volume 6, concerning the defeat of the proposal to contribute three battleships to the British Navy, the right hon. Prime Minister made use of the following language:
" As the construction of these ships is to be proceeded with by the British Government, as they are apparently to be of the same character, the same strength and the same fighting value as those which we proposed; as they are to be employed for the same purpose, that of the common defence of this Empire, which we had in mind, it is the firm intention and determination of this Government, if it remains, as undoubtedly it will remain In power, to bring down, at a later date, a proposal for the acquisition or construction of three battleships, as was proposed in the Naval Aid Bill of 1912. In that way, before the completion of these ships, we hope and expect to be in a position to say to the British Government: Canada is prepared to do now what the unworthy action of a partisan majority in the Senate prevented her from doing before; Canada will take over and pay for and acquire these ships and will place them at the disposal of His Majesty the King for the common defence of the great Empire of which Canada forms a part."
2. Have the ships above referred to been built?
3.	Is it the intention of the Government to make provision for the payment of these ships, as intimated by the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN NAVAL SERVICE.
speechtext: In the autumn of 1913 the Government had under consideration the re-introduction of the Naval Aid Bill of 1912, but thought such Te-intro-duction undesirable unless there was some reasonable prospect that it would not be defeated in the Senate. Confidential inquiries were made for the purpose of ascertaining whether such a Bill either in its original form or in some modified foTm might be expected to pass the Senate; thus enabling Canada to assume her proper share in maintaining the common defence of the Empire. It was reported to the Prime Minister as the Tesult of these inquiries that no assurance could be given of the acceptance by the Senate either of the Naval Aid Bill in its original form or of a modified, proposal which the Government were prepared to consider. For this reason no action was taken as it was thought undesirable to renew the controversy without any reasonable hope that the Government's proposal would be carried in the Senate. In 1914 with the view of formulating a permanent policy of naval defence it was arranged with the Admiralty that Admiral iSir John Jellicoe should visit Canada in August or September for the purpose of giving to the Government the benefit of his wide knowledge and experience. While arrangements for his visit were still in progress, the war broke out. Thereafter the Government ascertained that in the opinion of the Imperial authorities the efforts and resources of Canada should be concentrated during the present war upon the organization, training and equipment of military forces and that it would be inexpedient for the Canadian Government under the circumstances to undertake at present the provision of assistance in Naval Defence upon any considerable scale.

subtopic: EXPORT OF CANNED LOBSTERS.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: EXPORT OF CANNED LOBSTERS.
speechtext:
I have received an important letter which I would like to read to the House in the public interest, and especially for the information of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The letter is from one engaged in the lobster packing business, and the writer says:
In view of the possible embargo against shipments of canned lobsters and their importation into European countries, we are not at the moment anxious buyers for the coming season's pack. The uncertainty prevailing adds another difficulty to this year's business. The question of getting space for our goods in transatlantic
160i
steamers, high rates of freight prevailing, increased war risk charges, and the reduced rates of exchange prove a serious handicap to the business, and now this is further increased by the rumour that canned lobsters are likely to be considered among luxuries and therefore prohibited from Great Britain. Circulars from some of the English receivers have been received by many packers in these provinces during the past week. The fact that canned fruits are being classed as luxuries causes fear that canned lobsters because of their high price, will be so considered. We understand that the Department of Trade and Commerce is in communication with the Imperial authorities endeavouring to arrange so that all fish foods emanating from the colonies may not be discriminated against, but they are not yet in a position-so we are informed-to give us any satisfactory assurance on this point. You can readily see that if canned lobsters are prohibited from Great Britain, or if the steamship companies are instructed not to accept them as part of their freight that this will have a most disastrous effect upon the canned lobster business of 1916. Even the uncertainty that prevails causes a weakness in the market that renders a loss of revenue to the country itself.
In reference to the same matter, you will see by this morning's Citizen that the Hon. Reginald McKenna, Chancellor of the Exchequer, announced in the British House of Commons:
That the Government had resolved to deal with the importation of luxuries by stopping importation altogether rather than by tariffs.
Under the circumstances, I am sure that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be looking after the interests of a very important branch of industry in Canada if he would take this matter up, and see if the Imperial authorities would consent to exclude canned lobsters from the commodities refused entry into the United Kingdom.

subtopic: EXPORT OF CANNED LOBSTERS.
speechtext: Correspondence has already taken place with reference to this matter. I will do the best I can to try to persuade the British Government that lobsters are not luxuries, but if, in the end, it is their judgment that they are luxuries, and if they think it is of public importance that they should not be allowed into Great Britain, I suppose we shall have to abide by that decision, and make the best of it. The steamships will not take them if they are not allowed entry into Great Britain, but there will be no effort on the part of this Government to prevent the steamships carrying them until the attitude of the British Government has been, definitely ascertained. I do not think I can give my hon. friend any clearer answer in the meantime.

subtopic: EXPORT OF CANNED LOBSTERS.
speechtext: It is not very clear.

subtopic: DISTURBANCES AT WINNIPEG.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Hon. A. E. KEMP (Acting Minister of Militia and Defence):
subtopic: DISTURBANCES AT WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
On Monday my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition inquired with reference to an alleged riot of soldiers in Winnipeg. The District Officer Commanding at Winnipeg telegraphs as follows:
Militia Headquarters, Winnipeg, Man.,
April 4, 1916.
The Secretary,
Militia Council, Ottawa.
Yours third re disturbances. There has been no trouble since four o'clock on the 2nd instant. Immediate cause of trouble was arrest of three soldiers by the city police, on charge of being drunk and disorderly. The arrest caused a collection of crowd in which were a number of soldiers who attacked the police and released the soldiers. The police reserves were brought up, rearrest the soldiers and some civilians. In a few minutes a crowd of several hundred was collected and a running fight kept up between the police and the mob. Some street car windows were broken. Provost Marshall's piquet came up and endeavoured to restore order. City police charged them among the others, apA parently not noticing their police badges. Apparently this ended the matter as far as actual rioting was concerned. An hour or two later, however crowds collected again and wished to attack the police station. On Sunday the mob assembled about the police station and broke the windows, also took some prisoners away from the piquet. I placed about one thousand men in charge of the central section of the city and although the crowds to the extent of several thousands lined the sidewalks until late at night we'h'ad no trouble after four o'clock afternoon of the 2nd instant, and there has been none since. City patrolled by small piquets from various regiments have picked up all stragglers. Much of trouble occasioned by men on week end leave from outside battalions. This has been stopped for the future, also all bar rooms placed out of bounds for the present. Only men hurt were three duty men run into by fire department. They are doing well. Investigation being held; matter will be reported fully.

subtopic: DISTURBANCES AT WINNIPEG.
speechtext: There have been several instances of riots in which soldiers have taken part. Everybody recognizes that the majority of these soldifers are young men, and we can forgive them a great deal; but they must be taught that the first duty of a soldier is to maintain discipline. PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.

speechtext: On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), the House went into Committee on Bill No. 66, in aid of Provincial Legislation prohibiting or restricting the sale or use of intoxicating liquor®, Mr. Bhodes in the Chair.
On section 1-persons not to send liquor into provinces knowing or intending that it shall be dealt with unlawfully; penalty:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we had some considerable discussion in regard to this clause the other evening and a number of amendment? were suggested. I am not prepared to say that in regard to all of them they seem to me to be necessary to be made in this section. I am disposed to believe in regard to some of them that the wording of the section as it is in the Bill covered the cases sought to be met by the suggested amendments. But, there are one or two of them that I am disposed to believe it would be essential to add if we want to attain the object for which they were suggested. I am prepared to aoccapt certain of those suggestions, namely, the suggestion of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) that our Bill would be strengthened if, in the first clause, we added to the prohibitions as to sending, shipping, and so forth, the words " or cause to be sent or shipped." While I thought and still think myself that the words as they stood would have covered cases of that kind, that is of causing to be sent, etc. nevertheless it is true that in on analogous section of theCan-ada Temperance Act the words suggested by the hon. member axe contained and it is perhaps well to avoid any suggestions that because of a difference in the wording of the two sections a different result was intended or proposed. I intend therefore to amend the section by inserting in the second line, after the words " or carried " the words " or causes to be sent, shipped, taken, brought or carried. " That is the first modification I propose to make. Then there was also a suggestion that the Bill would he strengthened by making this clause 1 apply not only to people who send or carry the goods as already provided, but by making it also applicable to the man who sells goods with knowledge that they are to be sent or shipped or carried into a province in which there is prohibition for the purpose of violating the law. It was pointed out, and I may say that after the Bill had been printed it occurred to myself, that there might be an opening for an evasion of the law founded on the fact that in order to come within its terms a person would have to send, ship or carry, either by himself or his agents, the goods into the province in question. That evasion might come about by the person selling the liquor for that purpose and making such

an arangement that he might sell to some other individual who would do the sending, shipping or carrying, and the person so selling, although he was selling with a perfect knowledge of the purpose, would escape- certainly might escape-the application of the law. I propose therefore to add after the words " as aforesaid " in the I2th line the following:
Or shall sell or cause to he sold any intoxicating liquors knowing or intending that such intoxicating liquor will be sent, shipped, taken, brought or carried into any province from any other province or from any place outside of Canada and thereafter dealt with in violation of the laws of the province into which such in-intoxicating liquor is sent, shipped, taken, brought, carried or imported as aforesaid.
It was further suggested that we should provide for maximum as well as minimum penalties. I propose to do that by making a first offence subject to a fine of not less than $100 and not exceeding $200, and a second offence subject to a fine of not less than $200 and not exceeding $400.
The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) also suggested that there might be some difficulty as to the enforcement of the provision of the section which made the kegs, barrels, cases, bottles, packages, ot receptacles subject to forfeiture where an offence has been committed. The hon. gentleman suggested that a difficulty might arise if the section did not make the conviction itself a cause of forfeiture. I propose to meet that suggestion, which I think is a wise one, by substituting in line 32 for the words "such offence" the words "conviction" and for the word "committed" in the same line the word, "had." So that the provision in that regard will read:
And all intoxicating liquors with respect to which a conviction has been had, and all kegs, barrels, cases, bottles, packages or receptacles of any kind in which such liquor is contained, shall be forfeited.
And further by adding the words:
-and shall be destroyed or otherwise disposed of in such manner as the court may direct.
I propose to reach these results by moving to strike out, so that we may have it clearly before us, section 1 .as it appeared in the Bill and substitute a section such as it is in the Bill, (but with the modifications that I have already mentioned,. I beg to move that section 1 be struck out and the following substituted:
1. Any person who by himself, his clerk, servant or agent,
(a) shall send, ship, take, bring or carry or cause to be sent, shipped taken, brought or carried to or into any province from or out of

any other province or import into any province from any place outside of Canada any intoxicating liquor knowing or intending that such intoxicating liquor will or shall be thereafter dealt with in violation of the law of the province into which such intoxicating liquor is sent, shipped, taken, brought, carried or imported as aforesaid; or
(b) shall sell or cause to be sold any intoxicating liquor knowing or intending that such intoxicating liquor will be sent, shipped, taken, brought or carried into any province from any other province or from any place outside of Canada and thereafter dealt with in violation of the law of the province into which such intoxicating liquor is sent, shipped, taken, brought, carried or imported as aforesaid, shall be liable on summary conviction to a penalty for the first offence of not less than one hundred dollars and not exceeding two hundred dollars or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two months with or without hard labour, and for a second offence to a penalty of not less than two hundred dollars and not exceeding four hundred dollars or imprisonment for a term not exceeding four months with or without hard labour, and for a third and every subsequent offence to imprisonment for a term not exceeding less than six months and not more than twelve months with or without hard labour ; and all intoxicating liquor with respect to which any conviction has been had and all kegs, barrels, cases, bottles, packages or receptacles of any kind in which such liquor is contained, shall, upon such conviction, be forfeited and shall be destroyed or otherwise disposed of in such manner as the court may direct.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: It has been suggested to me that if the word " believing " were put in after " knowing and intending," it would make it wider.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I think that the purpose the hon. gentleman has in view is met by the next section, which creates a presumption that the man knew or intended, unless he proves the contrary. Section 2 says:
On any prosecution for the violation of this Act the accused person shall he deemed to have known or intended that such intoxicating liquor would he thereafter dealt with in violation of the law of the province into which such intoxicating liquor was sent, shipped, taken, brought, carried or imported, unless he proves that he had good reason for believing that the intoxicating liquor would only he dealt with in a lawful manner.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: This applies to prosecution for the violation of the Act for selling, carrying, and so on. Suppose that a company is the carrier.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: For the purpose of this Act, " person " covers not only a natural person but a fictitious person, a company.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
How are you going to
put a company in gaol for the third offence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The limit of our power would be to fine the company. I do not know of any way by which we can imprison a company.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Take the case of the
captain or the purser of a steamer that carries liquor; would he be guilty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I think our words are wide enough to apply to any individual who actually carries the goods in. Any person who knowingly violates the Act, I think, would not be entitled to escape on the plea that he acted as a representative of a company.-

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: How would it be in case the Government is the carrier? As a matter of fact, in our province the Government is the carrier of four-fifths of the goods, because these are carried on Government steamships or Government railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I think we must' assume that the Crown will not violate the law. The section will not apply to the Crown unless the Crown is specifically mentioned-that is a general rule of the interpretation of statutes. It would be unusual to mention the Crown specifically in a statute that is essentially of the nature of a criminal statute. I should say it would apply to an officer of the Government', who was knowingly carrying these goods.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Where the Crown has gone into the business of transportation, it would not reflect unduly upon the Government,-notwithstanding the respect we ought to have for the gentlemen occupying the Treasury benches-or upon the Crown or officers of the Crown, to provide expressly that this section shall apply to employees of the Intercolonial railway. As my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) says, all that the temperance people of Prince Edward Island have to fear in the way of transportation is in the operation of the Government railways and steamers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I did not suggest that employees of the Crown had any immunity. A person is not excused for committing an unlawful act by pleading that he is a Government employee. There is no irresponsibility on the part of employees of the Crown unless we specifically enact it, and that we are not doing. But the -purpose of making special mention of the Crown, as I understand it, would be to make the Crown liable to fine or imprisonment, and I hardly think that necessary.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: But the transportation can hardly be said to be effected by the employee. It is not the conductor or brake-man that transports the goods, but the railway company. If you brought up the conductor or brakeman charged with violation of this statute, he would say: I have nothing to do with the transportation; it is the company that does that. As to the Crown, my hon. friend knows that no statute will apply to the Crown unless the Crown is specifically named. I have seen *so imany judgments cf an extraordinary nature in my lifetime,-and I say that not to reflect upon the judges-

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Probably it was the result of the work of the lawyers who advised the judges.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Assuming that the prohibition in the province of New Brunswick is enforced in respect of the sale of intoxicating liquor and not against its importation for personal use, it seems to me that it would be unjust to the employees of the Government railways to require that they should know the purpose for which liquor is being sent into that province. The owners of the railway, that is to say, the Crown, ought to stand by the employee, if the employee should so accept liquor and so deliver it to the man who purposes using it himself. It would be absolutely unfair that the employee should be fined. I think that this matter deserves some consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
For the moment all we are concerned with is the first section, which imposes liabilities only on people who knowingly, knowing or intending that the law

is to be violated, carry this liquor. A person who is the employee of a railway is no more justified in committing the offence knowingly than is a person who is not the employee of a railway. It is no defence for a person charged with any violation of a law of this kind, which in its nature is analagous, to, if not absolutely a criminal law, to say: I committed the crime as the servant of somebody. It would not be suggested that the employee of a railway company which had sent its employees to steal my coal to run its engines could justify his action by saying:	I stole the coal, but I
was doing it only as agent of the railway company. So far as the protection of the employee is concerned, he is not liable to prosecution unless he knowingly, knowing or intending that there shall be a violation of the law, takes part in the operation. When we come to deal with the presumption, we shall be able to show that the position in which that employee would find himself would enable him to negative any presumption against him. It is difficult for me to conceive any circumstance under which he would not be able to show the court that personally or individually he had reason to suppose that everything was legal. There is a fair presumption in the very fact that the article is being publicly carried by a carrier with regard to whom responsibility under this Act would be clear. As to the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John that we should make this thing so clear that no magistrate should ever make a mistake in its application, I so thoroughly agree with his view of the fallibility of magistrates and judges that I renounce any advance to any such undertaking. The principle that the immunity of the Crown from the operation of a statute d,oes not apply to protect the employees of the Crown in violating a law of this nature is so clear that we can trust that it will be recognized. If we go so far as to put words into every statute so as to negative the possible error of any magistrate-well, this would be a very long Bill. It is not impressed on my mind that there is any special danger with regard to the particular matter that the hon. member for St. John points out.
Mr.: PUGSLEY: The Intercolonial railway does the whole of the transportation business in the northern section of the province of New Brunswick, and also between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, and through the larger part of Novia Scotia.

It is the great transportation system of a very considerable portion of the Maritime Provinces, operating, I think, something over 2,000 miles of road. The section says:
Any person who by himself, his clerk, servant or agent, shall send, ship, take, bring or carry to or into any province.
Let ms suppose that liquor is taken to the freight station of a railway company, put on board the train, and shipped to its destination in some other province. Would you say that the conductor of the train that carries it, the brakeman, the fireman, the engineer; would, you say that any one of these four employees is carrying that liquor? I say, no. It is the company that does it, through its officials.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Is not intent the essence of crime?

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I do not see that that has to do with the point I am raising just at the moirient. In my judgment, although you may sometimes find on the bench people as foolish as I am, and perhaps not knowing any more than I do, no court of any intelligence would hold that any one of these four persons is guilty of carrying that liquor. They are simply the 4 p.m. people who are operating the train for the time being. As the hon. member for Northumberland has said,, it would be most unjust to fine these people, because if they attempted to stop the train and throw that liquor off at some way station they would be dismissed very quickly by the general manager. It would be unjust to fine them under this section, because they are in no way responsible and in no way guilty of the offence with which this section is intended to deal. The minister could easily amend the Bill so as to impose liability upon the employees at the point of shipment or the employees at the point of reception, who would be the freight agents who are in charge of stations. But to say that employees who are running the trains should be liable would be most unjust.
Now as to the Crown. The Intercolonial have their freight department at Montreal. Some person takes a package containing liquor to their station in Montreal, consigned to some person in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island. It is very clear that the Crown would not be liable to a penalty unless the Crown was expressly mentioned. I do not think myself that the employees of the Crown would be liable unless the Crown was expressly mentioned, because the Crown can only act through its employees, and it has been held by the very highest authority that the Crown is not intended to be affected by a statute unless it is expressly mentioned in the statute. If the Crown would not be intended to be referred to or included in a statute unless expressly mentioned, neither, in my judgment, would the employees of the Crown be understood to be affected. The Intercolonial railway receives liquor at its freight station in Montreal, as I say, consigned to some place in New Brunswick or Nova Scotia. Is it intended that the employees operating the railway train that carries that liquor are to be liable to and subject to 3 fine? Suppose a brakeman going through the train sees a parcel consigned to some one in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick which he suspects contains liquor, and he sees upon it the address of some person who he thinks is engaged in the illegal sale of liquor. If that brakeman, assisting in the operation of the Intercolonial railway train, is brought up before a magistrate, the onus of proof is on him, because as a brakeman he had to do with the operation of the train bringing the liquor into some part of Nova Scotia, and he has got to prove to the satisfaction of the magistrate that he had reason to believe it was intended simply for the use of the consignee and not for sale. Then if the magistrate fined him, that would be most unjust. He is engaged in the operation of the Government railway, and he ought not to be fined because he would lose his position at once if he attempted to interfere with any article of freight carried on that railway. Therefore it seems to me that the minister, knowing as he does that the Crown is engaged in this vast system of transportation, ought to expressly mention the Crown, and make the principal officials of the Intercolonial at the points of shipment or the points of reception liable under this statute. If he dobs not do that he is going to make this law nugatory so far as a large portion of the Maritime Provinces is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I cannot undertake to legislate on the assumption that the Crown will proceed to' violate this law, and if I inserted the Crown in this law I would be proceeding on that assumption. Then, as the hon. gentleman has pointed out, the Crown always acts through its agents. It is not quite conceivable to me how you are going to assume that the 'Crown, which can do no wrong, has violated the provisions

of a criminal or quasi-criminal statute. As to the hon. gentleman's appeal for the innocent brakesman, I do not see how it can be suggested that the brakesman who is turning the brakes on a car is carrying anything, or sending anything or bringing anything. He will not have any presumption against him because there will be nothing proved. The presumption does not come into play except as regards the question, of his knowledge; all the rest has first to be affirmatively proved by the Crown. I have no doubt that if a man approaches an official of the Intercolonial railway and induces him to send liquor into a prohibition province to be sold in that province, and that official takes it and sends or carries it into the province, such an official could not shield himself behind his quality of employee to say: I did not violate the law. It is no defence for a man who commits a crime to plead that he did. it in his quality of somebody's employee, and there is no immunity for the employee of the Crown more than for the employee of anybody else, if he does commit an offence. But the man in connection with the Intercolonial who would be liable to prosecution under any circumstances is the man who, in some way, knowingly and intentionally handles and sends the stuff. To hold that the conductor is carrying the goods that are in a freight train would be beyond any conception I could form of the judgment of any magistrate. The railway company is doing the carrying, and unless you have an individual who knowingly, personally does something that contributes to it, he is not doing the carrying. But if you have a brakeman, or a conductor, or anybody else on the train, who carries liquor in violation of the tew, that man will be committing an offence.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Not unless it is for sale?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: In such a case that man would have to show, as any person else would, that he had reason to believe he was carrying the liquor for lawful purposes.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is speaking of a case in [DOT] which, in order to obtain a conviction, it must be shown that the person who received the liquor to be carried knows it is liquor. But this is how the thing is worked out on the Government railway to-day in places where we have the provincial law: A person in the city of Halifax sends a barrel of what are

called groceries and inside that barrel there may be a couple of cases of Scotch whisky. It is billed as groceries to the receiver, and it is afterwards sold to the people who desire to get whisky. Is there anything in this law which would permit of a conviction for taking or carrying liquor into a province under these circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: And that he knew he carried liquor?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Of course if there is a possible method which can be suggested or devised by which we can better reach any man who carries liquor, knowing he is carrying liquor, we will be glad to adopt it. In- the suggested amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver which I have already expressed my willingness to accept, v.e are going to try to mast the condition which the hon. member for Pictou speaks of, so far as it is possible to meet it. That is to say, we are going to make it an obligation on everybody who ships liquor into such provinces to plainly label it on the outside. To that extent we will compel the man who ships the liquor to inform the carrier. There will be instances in which men will not do it-

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The carrier may receive it without any marks, and it will be taken into the prohibited districts without anybody knowing of it until it reaches its destination.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman suggest what could be done further than to make it an offence to ship the liquor without publicly announcing what it is.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
My view is that you
must not assume that the Crown is going to be innocent of these things. Agents of the Crown carrying liquor in violation of the law would be guilty of an offence just as much as the agents or managers of the Canadian Pacific railway, Grand Trunk railway, or Canadian Northern railway. You must treat them all alike; you must

put the - Crown in exactly the same position as the railway companies. That, I hold, is absolutely essential, having reference to the condition of affairs in the Maritime Provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: If I mentioned the (Crown, I would not produce any different result as regards the employees. Furthermore, if I did, I would be doing a most extraordinary thing. Does the hon. gentleman suggest that we should insert the name of the Crown in the (Criminal (Code?

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
If they go into the
transportation business, why not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
My hon. friend may
he quite right, but, so far as my humble judgment goes I cannot accept his view. I am not prepared to -accept the suggestion that the Crown -should be mentioned in the Statute. As regards his suggestion that the manager of the Intercolonial, or of any *Government railway, will, under this Act, be in a different position- from the manager of the Canadian Pacific railway, unfortunately, I am not able to agree with him. I am quite convinced that the manager of the GOnterqalonial railway, if he knowingly accepts -for carriage, and carries these goods will be liable under this Act.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
He would not be
unless it was expressly mentioned that it was liquor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman contend that a Government employee shares the immunity of the Crown for criminal or quasi criminal offences?

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
If he performed
duties prescribed by the -Crown, could he not shelter himself under the privilege of the Crowm? I think that is sound law. If the Crown commands one of its employees to do a certain act, if the Minister of Jus-tics asks a certain officer in his department to do a certain act, that person does it as a direct representative of the Crown. Does -the minister say that the official could not plead the immunity of the Crown?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: 1 certainly say so if the thing I told him to do was a violation of the law of the country. It is a large feature of the protection of our liberties, that a man cannot plead an order of the Crown as justification for a violation of the law of the land. I am surprised-I think I may be pardoned for saying so-that the suggestion should be made. The hon. gentleman's argument comes to this: I may go into my department and send one of my clerks out to steal some object for the Crown, and then he may plead the immunity of the Crown. It is the real safeguard in our system that, while the Crown can do no wrong, an employee of the Crown cannot plead the instructions of his superior officer, any more than any other employee can plead the instructions of -his employer, as justification for his going out personally and violating the law of the land.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: My hon. friend says that if Mr. -Gutelius, the General Manager of the -Canadian -Government Railway, carried any liquor on his railway he could be proceeded against, provided, he says, that he knew thait he w-as carrying liquor. That is a very nice thing to say. My hon. friend knows that it would be -absolutely impossible to prove that Mr. -Gutelius knew anything about what was carried on the railway, -because he could not have personal knowledge unless he was present and knew something about the shipment. We come back to the point raised by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), that you could not proceed against Mr. Gutelius, or against any other official of the Intercolonial railway, who did not "know that it was liquor he was carrying. Is there anything in this Act to enable a prosecution to be successfully maintained against the man who delivers, which is the essential thing, at any point within a prohibited district, a certain box containing liquor or other article prohibited under the provincial law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
The hon. gentlehian seems to think that the employees of the Intercolonial railway should, he treated differently from everybody else,* and that I should make it an offence in the case of an employee of the Intercolonial railway who has nothing to do with the carrying oi liquor, or who, if he has to do with it, is not in a position to know anything about the contents of the package. I have not iiea-rd it suggested yet that we should make the manager of the Intercolonial railway criminally liable because some employee, of whom he has no knowledge, takes this liquor into the province unknowingly. There is nothing peculiar about the position of the employees of the Intercolonial, from the point of view of responsibility, as contrasted with the employees of any other railway company. This I do concede: that the Crown, the Intercolonial railway being

vested in the Crown, is not in the position of, say, the Canadian Pacific railway company. Save in so far as recourse under this Act against the company itself is concerned, there would be absolutely no difference between the working of this Act on the Intercolonial railway and its working on any other railway system. Unless some one commits the offences provided for under this'Act, we will not be .able to prosecute, and it is essential-I do not see how we can make it otherwise-to the commission of the offences, for which you are going to punish a. person, that he should have some knowledge that he is committing an offence.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I have not suggested that the Grown should be treated differently from railway companies. All I am insisting upon is that they should he treated exactly the same as the ordinary transportation companies. What I contend is that the employees of the Intercolonial railway-being a common carrier, though owned by the Crown-necessarily do the same business as the employees of ordinary railway companies. The same offence will be committed as will be committed toy the other railway companies. A company can toe fined and can be made to pay the fine under this statute. I presume also those who have special charge of the handling of freight at the point of shipment, and at the point of receiving, will be liable. Oan there be any objection to providing expressly that the Government railway, the managers and the employees, shall be in the same position as the railways and employees of private companies? That is all I suggest, and I think myself that in accordance with the principle of. law the Crown will not be deemed to be affected by a statute unless it is expressly named. Upon that principle, in so far as the carrying of liquors is concerned on the Government railway, I think the 'court would hold that the Government railways being owned by the Crown, it was not intended by Parliament to include them in its provisions. I do not see that the court could possibly do anything else in accordance with the general principles. It is so easy to make it plain that the management of the Intercolonial railway would be in the same position, and liable to the same penalty, as a railway company and 'its employees would he. When it is so easy to put that in I do not think it is any answer for the Minister of Justice to say that it will not be presumed that the 
Crown, which means the managers of the Intercolonial railway, will be guilty of a violation of the law. The Crown can only be guilty of an offence if its agents are guilty of an offence, and when my hon. friend knows that the agents 'and managers of these Government railways are just as apt to be guilty of an offence under the proposed statute as the managers and employees of a private railway company, he ought to make provision to meet the case which must necessarily arise in the transportation business of the Maritime Provinces. I admit he cannot provide that the (Crown shall suffer a penalty, or that the Crown shall pay a fine, but he can provide that for any offence against this statute the managers and employees of the Intercolonial railway shall be liable equally as the managers and employees of any private transportation company shall be liable. My hon. friend knows that for a great many years in this country it was held before the law was changed, that the Crown could not be sued, on the theory that the Crown could be guilty of no wrong. It took a long time before Parliament came to a realization of the fact that it would be only just to give an individual the right of action against the 'Crown. Previously it was supposed that the only proper remedy was to apply by petition of right to the grace and favour of His Majesty. That has all been done away with and to-day, in the case of small claims, .at all events, the subject is allowed to bring action .against the 'Crown and to have it tried in the ordinary courts of the country. I think action is brought against the general manager.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: First the managing board and then the general manager.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Yes, the general manager. My hon. friend knows the general manager previous to this Change in the law could not be sued for any wrong which was -done in the operation of the Government railways. ;A Government railway locomotive might, by reason of a .spark being carried by the wind across the track and into the field of a private individual, destroy that individual's building, or his forest and. there was no liability. I doubt if there is any liability to-day unless the fire actually starts upon the Intercolonial railway itself and spreads to the property of the individual. I think we ought to do away with this old idea that the Crown is .supposed not to do any wrong and not to be liable in damages and that the in-

dividual ought simply to 'look to the grace and favour of the Crown. When t'he Crown has gone into the transportation business, the same as an ordinary railway or steamboat company, we ought to expressly include Government railways in the Bill and expressly place the management of the Intercolonial, and the officers and employees of that railway, on the same basis as the managers and employees of any ordinary railway or steamboat company engaged in the transportation business.
Mr. LOGGIE; The minister mentioned that by another section of the Bill he would make it imperative that a package shall be labelled "intoxicating liquor." Might I suggest to him that there would be a certain safeguard if the shipper would attach to the way bill, or to the bill of lading, a certificate to the effect that the consignee made the statement that the liquor was for his personal use?

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Would he not do that in any case? The railway company would provide its own rules.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: We would be more likely to make some progress with the Bill if we would deal with the matters that arise under the present section. When the suggested amendments come we can discuss the effect of those amendments. I do not want to curtail discussion at all but we should get along as systematically as we * can and confine ourselves to the matters that are before us.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: There seems to be a difference of opinion between the Minister of Justice, the hon. member for St. John, and the hon. member for Pictou as to the effect of the law on officers of the Government. I do not wish to enter into that discussion or to say who is right or who is wrong, but the illustration which the minister gives shows that he is not on the right track. He compares the situation to a case where he as a minister of the Crown sends out a servant with instructions to steal from some one; and he says that the man would be liable. Granted that he would, does not the minister see the tremendous difference? The servant Whom he sends out is sent out to do something that is not in the ordinary course of his business. But in the other case the man is acting in the ordinary course of his business; under instructions, and therefore there could be no comparison between the two cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
He could never in the
ordinary course of business commit a crime.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I shall not argue that
point further. If I understand this section correctly; it provides for the punishment not only of the individual but also of a company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
You will have to get
that combination of circumstances which it is not quite easy to get in regard to a corporation where you can bring home to the company itself, the actual showing and intending certain things to be done. I cannot make this law more general than by providing for its application to every person.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The minister is entirely astray as to my intention; perhaps I have not been plain enough in my statement. I wish to refer to the punishment for a third offence. It seems that under this section the punishment is provided for a' first and .second offence by a company, but there is no way to punish a company for a third offence. Would my hon. friend have any objection to adding something which would provide a penalty in the case of a third offence? An individual who .offends the third time must be imprisoned. Could he not make provision that in the case of company a very heavy pecuniary penalty may be inflicted? I presume it is the intention to punish the man who receives liquor, knowing that it is going to be used for an improper purpose, as well as the sender. I am not quite sure that the wording is clear on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The receiver will be the person in the province in which the provincial prohibition law is in force, and the provincial law will take care of him. The reason we are legislating is to get at people who are outside of the province, and therefore not governed by the provincial prohibition law. The man who receives liquor in violation of the law of the province will be taken care of by the law of that province.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: If that is quite clear, I am satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: When I say he will be taken care of, it depends, of course, on whether the province legislates. At all events, the province has him right under * its hand.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Trade and commerce, of course, comes undeT the jurisdiction of the Dominion Parliament; and

if an importer comes under trade and com- . meroe, and there is any question as to the right of the province to punish him, my hon. friend could meet that by simply adding " or who imports or receives."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I think this covers the importer, because our legislation is applicable to everybody who carries or takes liquor into the province, or who brings it in or causes it to be brought in. So if there is any danger of the province not being able to get the man within the province who does import, he will come under our legislation, because he will have caused the liquor to be brought in. It was suggested the other evening that the Bill would be strengthened by adding the words " or who causes to be brought into the province," and we have adopted that suggestion, but the words do not appear in the printed Bill. Personally, I think myself that the man who imports liquor would come under the head of the man who brings it in, even without these additional words; but with these additional words, there is, I think, no doubt that' the man who imports it is the man who causes it to be brought into the province.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
The words
" take " and " bring " are both in the printed Bill, and it struck me that a judge, when construing the section, would be liable to say that the intention was to cover merely the bringing in of liquor in the way that a carrier would bring it in; and I think he might be justified in interpreting it in that way. If the intention is to cover the importer, why not add " who receives or imports."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: What is it the importer does, except to bring liquor into the province or cause it to be brought in? I do not like to multiply repetitions of words that mean the same thing. We have used the word " importer " in the Bill, and I should like to reserve that word for designating the person who imports from outside the Dominion. I think we have covered the case when we add the words "or who causes to be brought into the province."

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
The man who brings it
in can be prosecuted, as well as the seller?
* Mr. DOHERTY: Yes. We want to make that quite clear. We do not want to leave him to the provincial law, because it might be said, even when he was caught with the liquor in his possession, that the bringing of the liquor across the line put

him outside the provincial law. So we cover the case of the man who brings the liquor into the province, takes it in, carries it in, brings it in, or causes it to be brought in.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: A seller living outside the Dominion, in Buffalo, for instance, would not come under the law at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: No, I am afraid we would not be able to catch him.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Who will bring the prosecutions under the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: We are making no special provision for that, but we are providing as to the places at which prosecutions may be brought, and we are making them susceptible of being brought within the prohibition province; that is to say, though my offence, supposing I committed one, may be in the province where I sell the liquor or send it from, under a subsequent provision it is enacted that I may be prosecuted in the province where the liquor was sent to. That puts it within the power of the prohibition province, or of the authorities or people living in that province, to bring about a prosecution against the man who does not reside within the province. We leave the laying of information under the general law. Any one may do that who has knowledge that an offence has been committed, and the case may be proceeded with as ordinary violations of the provincial law, or as violations of a statute of this nature are proceeded with.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: We know from experience that the enforcing of a prohibitory law is left pretty much to people who organize themselves into a body for that purpose, and it is pretty expensive. It is rather hard to expect these people to bring proceedings when they are doubtful as to the result of the action. As the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has said, the result of an action against the Crown or the Intercolonial railway would be very doubtful.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I think we agreed that there would be no doubt as to the result.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
The freight agent at the receiving point is the man above all others who would have knowledge of the offence, particularly if the package was marked and plainly showed to whom it was addressed. The freight agent would also b'e able to form a pretty good idea from the party who was making the shipment. I think it would

be a good idea to mention him in the Bill. The Government Railways Small Claims Act specifies the general manager as the one against whom an action may be brought, and I think that mentioning ari official in this way makes him take greater precautions. If an action can be brought with fair prospects of success against the officials of the Government, I think greater care would be exercised by them at all events. My own judgment is that, unless something .of that kind is done, so .far as the province of 'Prince Edward Island is concerned, this Act would be of very little use to prevent importation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
In my own judgment,
the freight agent referred to will be like every other citizen of Canada. If he knowingly ships that liquor, or causes it to be shipped, he will be liable to prosecution. If I mention that freight agent specially, and do not mention every other officer of the Intercolonial, I shall be open to the suggestion that by the mention of the one I intend to exclude the other. With all deference to the opinion of the hon. member for St. John, my opinion is that my Bill applies to everybody in Canada, including that freight agent and all the other employees

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: If you mention the general manager, you include them all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: It includes the general manager now. This is criminal or quasicriminal legislation. It is not to be compared with the small claims legislation in which the general manager is designated as the party to the suit. That does not mean that the general manager is to pay the money if the suit is lost; it simply gives a figurehead to avoid a petition of right in instituting proceedings against the Crown, and if the prosecution succeeds, the Crown pays. There is no analogy between that case and this. It would not be suggested that Mr. Guteliua should be made liable to be fined, or sent to jail because some freight agent, without his knowledge or consent, violated the law. Everybody will have to stand on his own personal responsibility, so far as violation of the law is concerned.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Not being a lawyer, I do, not propose to discuss the legal phase of this matter. But if there is anything in ' what my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) claims-and it certainly sounds reasonable-this Act will! be of very little
service. For, in addition to the Intercolonial railway, we have the Transcontinental between the East and Winnipeg, under control of the Government. It looks very much as if the Government would have to take over the Canadian Northern in a very short time, and if, besides, they have to take over aleo the Grand Trank Pacific from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert, something over half the railways, of the country will be in the hands of the Government. Then, if the contention of my hon. friend from St. John is right, this law will be practically a dead letter, so far ae half the country is concerned. Even if that hon. gentleman is altogether wrong in his legal opinion on this matter, the law will be a dead letter anyway, for the Minister o'f Justice does not propose to appoint anybody to see to the carrying out 'of the law. In Saskatchewan, when the law for partial prohibition was passed-when the bars were done away with-the Government, knowing that if the work of laying information were left to the general public it would be a difficult matter to have the law carried into effect, simply because what is everybody's business is nobody's business, and people do not like to become informers or prosecutors, appointed a public prosecutor, so that anybody who has belief that the law is being violated need simply drop a line to the public prosecutor who then sends his detectives or whatever force he thinks best to find out the facts. Then, if there has been violation, the public prosecutor takes action at once. The result is that so far, at all events-and the law has been in force since the 1st o'f July last-where there have been infractions of the law, the guilty parties have been very quickly got at and punishment has been severe in a number of cases. Ip that way, the law is being well observed. Now that the minister sees the difficulties standing in the way, would not it be advisable for him to withdraw this Bill, which, after all, is only a sidestepping Bill to get clear of Dominion-wide prohibition, and take the legislation suggested by the member for Vancouver. That would be more in the interest of the whole Dominion. That is what the people are asking for and, it is what they would be much more interested in carrying into effect than this quasi-legislation which it will be nobody's business, nobody's duty, except in a general way, to look after the enforcement of. The measure will not bring about any result, in my opinion, ex-

cept that of getting the Government out of a present difficulty.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: It has been suggested to me that (this first clause would not cover the case of a brakeman or conductor on a railway, or a captain of a steamboat. It says: "Any person who by himself, his clerk, servant, or agent, shall send," and so on. The clerk or agent might not be liable, but only the person who employed him. When the Prince Edward Island law was put in operation, in 1900, these words were used, but subsequently an amendment was passed, which would cover any person who sold the liquor. If th-e words: "by himself, his clerk, servant, or agent," were struck out, it would cover any person who brought in the goods. 1 do not know whether or not that is a proper interpretation of the law, tout I am making the suggestion, which has been made to me. If the conductor knew that the liquor was brought in for illegal purposes, would he, in the opinion of the minister, be liable, or would his principal only be liable?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: If the conductor took any personal part whatever in the handling of this liquor and bringing it in he would be liable. But the conductor, as I understand it, does not determine what is to be put in or what is not. 1 do not think the hon. gentleman wants to suggest that the conductor of a railway train, who has no control over these express packages, ought to be compelled to find out what is in them. He is not actually carrying them. As to the suggestion that anything would be gained by striking out the words " by himself or his agent," we are putting these words in only to make it clear that any person who, either himself or through his agents does this thing shall be liable to the provisions of this legislation. To take these words out would limit the application of the Bill, not extend it in the slightest.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: It is the superintendent of the railway, then, who would be liable, and he alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
No, it would be the
person or persons who knowingly took part in the carrying. If the superintendent of the railway knows absolutely nothing about the facts, we will not send him to jail because the conductor, for instance, took the liquor from me and carried it. In that case the conductor would be responsible; if the superintendent took it from me and FMr. Turriff. 1
gave me a bill of lading, the superintendent would be responsible. The person who does the thing will be responsible. I regret that I do not agree with the view of tbe hon. member for St. John, and that therefore I do not apprehend the ineffectiveness of this Bill as he suggests. When the Canadian Northern and all the other railroads that the hon. gentleman had in mind as being vested in the Dominion are passed over to this Government, every employee of these roads will be in just the same position under this Act as he was before. As to the distinctions sought to be made between the action of the Government of Saskatchewan and the action taken in connection with this Bill, I would point out, in the first place, that the administration of justice is the business of the provinces. Our duty is done when the law is made; the whole criminal law is administered by provincial authority. In the second' place, I should think that the province of Saskatchewan, which is so anxious to see its own law respected that it has provided a prosecutor to see that it is respected, would be only too glad to see that this legislation, made for the purpose of protecting the effectiveness of the provincial legislation, is enforced' and carried out. The hon. gentleman suggests that after I have seen all the difficulties I may withdraw the Bill. I must say that although I have heard a large number of suggested difficulties, I do not as yet perceive one, so that I see no reason why I should withdraw this Bill. This is not the time to discuss the principle of the Bill or to meet the suggestion that there is any sidestepping about it: Personally, I am quite satisfied that, if the provinces do their duty, we are, in proceeding in this way, assuring a much more effective prohibition measure than we would if rwe had proceeded by Dominion legislation. As to the hon. gentleman's assurance of what it is that the people want, I could, show him communications that I thave received from people who have spent their lives in the promotion of temperance, whose sincerity cannot be doubted, and who express the greatest satisfaction with this proposed legislation.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
One of the difficulties with this Bill is the failure of the minister >
to provide any means of enforcing the law after it is passed. The provinces do not require any assistance from us so far as enforcing their provincial legislation is

ooncerned. We are attempting here to make it an offence for a person in any other province to ship liquor into a dry province. Suppose a merchant in the city of St. John ships a package of liquor to the town of Guysborough. If the liquor were sold by a local dealer in Guysborough, all that the people would have to do would be to go .before the stipendiary magistrate or two justices of the peace and prosecute him. But horw are the (people of that municipality to carry on a prosecution against a merchant in the city of St. John?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Just go and lay information before the stipendiary magistrate right in the local place. That is provided for by another section. If the hon. gentleman would let us proceed section by section, we would more readily meet these difficulties.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The reason I spoke was that the minister himself referred to this matter in his remarks to the committee. In 1908 a large number of counties in Canada adopted the Scott Act, and it was regarded as a grievance that people outside of the Scott Act area were shipping liquor into counties where the Act had been adopted. The temperance people approached the Dominion Government of that day and a law was enacted making it a crime to ship or send liquor into counties in which the Scott Act had been adopted. I am familiar with the working of that law, and I do not know of a single case in which prosecution has been successfully carried on outside the province or county into which the liquor had been sent. It is practically impossible for the people in the locality where the provincial Act is in force to get at the party outside. That work should be undertaken by the minister's department, so that when a dealer in an outside province ships liquor into a province that has adopted prohibition the party aggrieved may go to the Department of Justice and have the Solicitor General or some authority in the department carry on the prosecution. If the minister will agree to a proposal of that kind, he will give us a workable Act that will be of some use. If he refuses to do so, I am very much inclined to think that his Act will be a dead letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I am sorry the hon.
gentleman tells us that the provinces, which aTe so anxious to have their own legislation effectively protected, do not care enough about it to carry out a law when we give
it to them. The hon. gentleman contrasts the facility of going to the stipendiary magistrate or two justices of the peace and laying information under the provincial law with what has to be done under this law. If he had waited to rqad the third section of this Bill, he would have seen 5 p.m. that just the same thing could be done under that section. But he must deal with this on the first section; he will not read the third one; he builds his whole grievance on the supposed difference between the tribunal to whom application will have to be made for the enforcement of this law and that under which application is to be made for the enforcement of the provincial law. It is true that you may have to send outside of the province to get the man, but that is true of all offences that are committed within a province, if the fellow gets outside. Does the hon. gentleman ignore the fact that the enforcement of the entire criminal law, so far as it depends upon Government, is the duty and business of Provincial Governments? It is not the function of this Government to administer justice; it is the function of Provincial Governments. I do not see what there is in this law which should call for a shifting from the shoulders of Provincial Governments of the responsibility for the performance of. their duty. I should say, on the contrary! that the very nature of this law makes it peculiarly the' business of Provincial Governments to see to its enforcement, because this is a law to protect the provinces in the enforcement of their own laws.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
The minister talks as if this Government were conferring a tremendous favour on the provinces when it passes a statute to assist the provinces in enforcing prohibition. You would think from the way he talks that this Parliament had no interest whatever in prohibition, no interest in improving the condition of affairs throughout the Dominion, and that when it simply puts upon the statute book a law which will the better enable the provinces to enforce prohibition, it does a wonderful thing, for which it is entitled to the gratitude of the provinces, and that there is no obligation upon this Parliament or this Government to go to tlie slightest expense towards seeing that the law is enforced^ This being a Dominion law, I do not see why this Government does not go to some expense in enforcing it. I quite agree with the minister that the punishment of crime in the different prov-



inces belongs to the provincial authorities. That is quite true. But this law, while it provides for the punishment of offences in which one province may be especially interested, provides also for the punishment of offences in other provinces. For instance, if a distiller in Ontario improperly jships liquor into Prince Edward Island, that distiller may be punished. But the minister says: Oh, let the Government of Prince Edward Island go up to Ontario and employ officers there to prosecute distillers in Ontario. Does not my hon. friend see that this is different from the ease of an ordinary criminal law in respect to which offences in a province are dealt with by the authorities of that province? It does seem to me that where the minister recognizes that it is desirable to make it an offence on the part of a shipper in a distant part of the Dominion to send liquor into a province to be used contrary to the law of that province it would not be unreasonable for the Dominion . Government to take authority to appoint public prosecutors whose duty it would be to see that the Dominion law is enforced. I quite agree with the hon. member for Guysbor-ough on the desirability of having prosecutors for the purpose of enforcing the law, and that unless that is done this law is likely to be an absolute dpad letter.
