The Minister of Justice has not lived in a section of Canada where there has been a prohibitory law." Those of us who come from New Brunswick know that we have had the Scott Act in force for a great many years. When it was brought into operation, twenty years or more ago, there was an earnest desire to enforce it. The temperance people went to large expense; they employed counsel; they organized} they put their hands in their own pockets to provide funds in an attempt to enforce the law. But they naturally became tired, after a while, of bearing these burdens, and there -are places in New Brunswick to-day where the Scott Act is a dead letter, whereas fifteen or twenty years ago it was vigorously enforced. To-day in many places fines are regularly imposed by common consent, and those fines take the place of license, and the prohibitory law is a dead letter; whereas when the law was first brought into operation it was vigorously enforced. If you are going to enfosee the law satisfactorily and continuously and effectively, you must have public prosecutors paid by the Dominion, whose duty it will be to assist the provinces m 
the enforcement of the law. When it is brought to the attention of this prosecutor that some distiller in Ontario is violating this law by sending liquor down into Prince Edward Island, that public prosecutor should take the necessary proceedings for the punishment of the offender. Unless you have some such system as that, this law is going to bd a dead letter, and I think that as, notwithstanding a very strong sentiment in favour of Dominion-wide prohibition, many of the members of this Parliament have yielded thefr views in regard to Dominion-wide prohibition and are supporting the Government

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman believe in Dominion-wide prohibition?

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I am in favour of this Bill, but there are many gentlemen who are strongly wedded to Dominion-wide prohibition.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Do you believe in it?

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I am in favour of this
Bill in preference to Dominion-wide prohibition.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman has answered my question.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I am in favour of this
Bill in preference to Dominion-wide prohibition. I stated-that the other day; my hon. friend perhaps did not hear me. What I say is that, when many gentlemen in this House, who have been strongly in favour of Dominion-wide prohibition, who feel that it would be far preferable to pass a law for Dominion-wide prohibition rather than to pass this law, the very least that they can ask the Government to do would be to pass a law to assist the provinces in the enforcement of prohibition; the very least the Government can do is to provide a reasonable sum for the appointment of a public prosecutor who will see that the law is carried out. I say'that the experience of the past 25 years in the different provinces of Canada where they have had prohibition under local option proves that you must have public prosecutors to carry out the law, and surely this Dominion, which provides that offences may be punished outside of the province immediately affected, can well afford to go to the expense of providing officers to enforce the law. This Parliament represents the whole people of Canada, who are interested in the enforcement of law, and it should take measures to see that the law which it enacts is en-

forced, and as I have said, it can only be enforced through public officials whose duty it is to see that it is enforced. Laws which axe not enforced, which are simply put on the statute-book to satisfy people who do not seem to be so much concerned in the enforcement of law as in having a law on. the statute-book, simply excite contempt among the people for all law, and, unless this Government is prepared to take the necessary steps to enforce the law, I think they had better not enact it at all, because it will prove, in the end, to be almost a dead letter and will do more harm than good to the cause of temperance.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-accused must prove that he had good reason for believing liquoT would not be dealt with illegally:

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I wish to move, with the approval of the Minister of Justice, who, I think, has already stated that he would consent to it, that the amendment, of which I gave notice, be inserted in the Bill as clause 2. Clause 2 would then read:
In addition to any other penalties prescribed for a violation of section one of this Act any person holding a license to carry on the business or trade of a distiller or brewer, issued under the provisions of the Inland Revenue Act, who violates the provisions of section one of this Act, or who sells or delivers intoxicating liquor in violation of the law in force it) afny province, shall also he liable in any prosecution under this Aqt, on conviction for a first offence, to the suspension of such license for any period not exceeding three months, and on conviction for a second offence, to the suspension of his license for any period not exceeding six months, and on conviction for a third offence, shall forfeit his license and shall thereafter be unable to hold such a license.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I have given consideration to the suggested amendment, and I am quite pleased to welcome it into the Bill. I think it is on the lines of the measure, as originally proposed, and is, I believe, likely to be a very effective protection against the violation of this Act, or of any provincial legislation, by persons who happen to hold licenses as distillers or brewers under the Inland Revenue Act.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I am very glad to know that the minister has decided to accept the amendment offered by my hon. friend from Vancouver, but after all it is only a half measure, or a half proposal. It proposes to penalize any brewer or distiller who commits a breach of the prohibitory liquor law which any province of Canada may adopt. They are penalized already,
or will be -by any provincial laws which may be enacted, and the mere fact of their being brewers or distillers will not free them from liability under the provincial statutes. If they break the law they can be fined.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: But they cannot suspend their licenses.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The only addition to the penalties would be that proposed now by my hon. friend from Vancouver in -the way of suspension of their license. I have always understood that the prohibitionists of Canada have -always considered that the manufacture within, and importation into the provinces of Canada are the chief defects in any scheme or system of provincial prohibition of the liquor traffic. In memorials and petitions to this House, -and to other public bodies, you will find that universally they ask to prohibit the manufacture and importation. In the Bill, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice attempts to deal with one branch of that request only, importation. Until the amendment was moved by my hon. friend from Vancouver, the Minister of Justice made no attempt whatever to do anything with regard to the manufacture. He proposed what in my judgment is hut a half measure, which will not- satisfy the vast majority of the people of this cc untry who are today asking foT -prohibitory liquo-r laws.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: You hope not, 1 suppose.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I hope it will, but I am satisfied that a half measure -is little better than no measure at all. So long as you permit the manufacture of liquor within the provinces, there is going to be sale, and illegal sale and consumption of that liquor. That is the view of the people who seek this legislation, and that certainly is my view. In the legislation which is being passed in the provinces, there is no doubt that the enactments are hitting the hotel keeper and the liquor store keeper. These interests are -being soaked by present or proposed legislation in the provinces; the manufacturer, the brewer and the distiller, are practically being left unaffected. Why not, in this measure, take the other step, and stop manufacture in the provinces which have passed, or are about to pass, prohibitory liquor laws. We can do it; this House has the power to do it, and I have just drafted a proposal, by way of amendment, which I desire to submit

to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice; and I would ask him to consider it. It may be that I will have to move it and divide the House upon it. I have drafted it hastily, and perhaps it may not be entirely free from objection, so far as the language employed is concerned. I have drafted it as follows:
No license shall hereafter be granted or renewed under the provisions of the Inland Revenue Act to any person to enable such person to carry on business as a distiller, brewer, or maltster in any province wherein a provincial Act is in force prohibiting the sale of intoxicating liquor.
Section 15 of the Inland Revenue Act provides for the issue of licenses to brewers, distillers, and maltsters. These are annual licenses which expire on the 30th June each year. Consequently, they will all run out on the 30th June next. If the .amendment, suggested is adopted, no brewers', distillers', or maltsters' licenses could be renewed in any province which has passed a law prohibiting the sale of intoxicating liquors. If this House will adopt an amendment of this kind, it will satisfy the great bulk of public opinion in Canada to-day, and it will do more for the adequate and proper' enforcement of those provincial laws than any other restriction, or any other legislation, which could be suggested by any hon. members of this House. I offer this merely as a suggestion to the Minister of Justice, and I ask him to consider it. I trust he will favourably consider it; if not, we might have a division and take the sense of the House upon it later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Before saying anything about the suggestion of my hon. friend, I would point out that we have before the Chair the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver to insert in the Bill the clause which he proposes. It is quite true that this measure does not deal with the manufacture of liquor. I explained the other evening the reasons which led me to believe that it was not necessary to do so in this measure, and I pointed out that, to introduce into this measure provisions with regard to the manufacture of liquor on the assumption that tile Dominion Parliament alo*ne can deal with the subject of manufacture, would be a departure from the principle of the Bill. That principle is legislation for the protection of the effectiveness of provincial legislation from outside interference. I do not wish to repeat again-I do not think anything would be gained by doing so-what I said the

other evening with regard' to the question of the manufacture of liquor, and to the measure of the power of the provincial legislatures in relation thereto. In my judgment, they certainly have a measure of power- in that regard. Their lordships of the Privy Council have said so. No Provincial Legislature as yet, has seen -fit to exercise, nor do I understand there is any proposition for any Provincial Legislature to exercise, such a measure of power in regard to the control of manufacture as they may possess. Until they have done that, if we are to be consistent with the principle of legislation that this House adopted the other night and with the principle of this very measure, the time is not yet come, if indeed it ever should come, when this Government, even if any action by this Government would be necessary to supplement Provincial Legislation in regard to manufacture, a question which it is not necessary to deal with now, should deal with the question. I am not prepared to depart from the principle of this measure, endorsed as it has been by the House, for the purpose of enacting a substantial, direct prohibition measure by this Dominion Parliament in the exercise of its prohibitory power. I reiterate the view which I entertained the other evening as to the necessity of this Parliament's action in order to deal with the question of manufacture. There is no purpose to be served by tmy repeating but I do entertain a very strong conviction that there is a very large measure of power in the Provincial Legislatures to deal with the question of the manufacture of liquor within- the provinces-.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The propriety has always -been recognized of this Government prohibiting the manufacture of intoxicating liquors in certain parts of the Dominion of Canada irrespective of other parts. That is specially provided for in the Inland Revenue Act. We know that there was a time when, in the Northwest Territories, there was prohibition while there was no prohibition in the rest of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: There was no Provincial Legislature in the territories then.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Clause 6 of the Inland Revenue Act provides:
No license shall be issued under this Act,- That is, to brewers, distillers and maltsters.	,
-nor shall any business subject to excise be carried on in any unsurveyed or unsettled tract

of country, or in any district or place prohibited by Order in Council.
So that it was always contemplated by Parliament that one section of the country might be designated by Order in Council and that in that section no license for a brewer, distiller or a maltster should be granted. By Order in Council, the present Government, without any further legislation, can provide that in any province where prohibitory legislation has been enacted no license shall be granted to a brewer, distiller or a maltster.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I do not suggest that
we have not power to do that.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: As I understood by hon. friend's remark a night or two ago he questioned very much the propriety of refusing a license, or of prohibiting manufacture in one province while it was permitted in another. But evidently that was in the contemplation of the framers of the Inland Revenue Act, and this power is really there and can be exercised by Order in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
What was suggested to me the other evening was that this House should enact Dominion legislation and make its effectiveness entirely dependent upon provincial legislation; that we should pass some general measure of prohibition or manufacture to be applicable only where a province had enacted certain prohibitory measures; in other words, legislation not for the entire Dominion. The Act that is cited is legislation governing the issue of licenses as regards the whole Dominion. Among the conditions that are fixed is one that they may not be issued in certain districts which are named. Throughout the Dominion as a whole authority is given the Governor in Council not to issue licenses in certain parts of the Dominion. But it is not linked up with provincial legislation, and the non-issuance of licenses is not made to rest upon the legislative action by particular provinces. I am quite prepared to say that I do not dispute the power of this Parliament to prohibit manufacture, and perhaps it is necessary, but I must confess to serious doubts of our authority, in the exercise of our power to prohibit manufacture, to deal with the question sectionally. The Privy Council, in maintaining the power of this Parliament to enact prohibitory legislation, so maintained it because it held that under certain conditions the evil could be looked upon as a Dominionwide, or national, evil, and because so considered the .subject was one properly
to be dealt with by the Parliament of the country as coming under the head of legislation for - the jieace, order and good government of Canada. The Privy Council on the other hand has held that this matter might be looked upon as a local evil in the province and that, if it is so looked upon, so long as the Dominion has not exercised its legislative power on the subject, the province might deal with the abatement of that evil, treat it as a local or provincial evil within the province, and enact such measures as in its judgment are necessary for the abatement of the evil. In that condition I think it would be very unwise for us to introduce into this House legislation which, in my judgment, at all events, is quite safe as against any attack for unconstitutionality, prohibiting manufacture and making our prohibition effective only in spots, so to speak, and making its effectiveness dependent upon provincial legislation and that effectiveness itself only existent within the areas of particular provinces.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Is that not what you are doing by this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Absolutely and totally
different. As I pointed out the other evening, this Bill makes it identically the same offence wherever the act is committed within the limits of this wide Dominion.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
It depends where
they send the liquor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: But the act can be done anywhere in this Dominion. The enactment is that for a man anywhere in this Dominion to bring about a violation within any province of a provincial law upon the subject of the sale of liquor is to commit an offence. This law is in effect throughout the whole Dominion, and no man anywhere in the Dominion can do that thing without being guilty of a crime.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: What my hon. friend overlooks is this: a man could arrange to send liquor into a certain province, and the sending into that province might not be a crime; but it might be a crime to send the liquor into another province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
That is one of the conditions of the offence. But what is the proposition of the hon. member for South Wellington? It is that there should be a direct substantive law of this Dominion, which law itself, in virtue of its being

the law of this Dominion, should make it a crime for a man to manufacture liquor, say in the province of Ontario.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I am only asking that no licenses be granted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Well, then, he is asking that it be made unlawful for any man to manufacture liquor in Ontario.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: In a province where there is provincial prohibition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Certainly. Let us be absolutely exact. The proposition of my hon. friend is that we should enact a law which will produce this result: that if the province of Ontario passes a prohibitory law, it will be unlawful, in virtue of the enactment of the Dominion Parliament, to manufacture liquor in Ontario, while at the same time it would be absolutely lawful under the general law of this Dominion to manufacture liquor in Quebec.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Now how does that differ in principle from the fact that it may be unlawful to import liquor into Ontario, we will say, and yet absolutely lawful to import liquor into Quebec or New Brunswick, where there is no prohibitory law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: It differs in this respect, that the Act which we are making unlawful will be unlawful anywhere in the Dominion, and the principle of it is that you cannot conspire anywhere in the Dominion to bring about something which, when it gets into that province, will be a violation of the provincial law. We are asked to pass a law to make unlawful in Ontario something that the Ontario law does not prohibit; namely, the manufacture of liquor. We are asked to make unlawful a thing which is not unlawful by the law of the particular province concerned.

maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Are you not by this Bill prohibiting importation into a province whose legislature has not prohibited importation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PBOHIBITION OE BESTEICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUOES.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
We are prohibiting the doing of something outside of that province. We are dealing with men outside the province right throughout this Dominion. What we are saying is: You shall not anywhere in the Dominion set to work to contrive to bring about the violation of provincial law. That is ah entirely different proposition. The hon. member for South Wellington assumes that the province either cannot or will not-I think he assumed that the prbv-ince cannot-prohibit the manufacture of

liquor; as it cannot, it does not; therefore, the manufacture of liquor, so far as the provincial law is concerned, is a lawful thing. Oh, no, the hon. gentleman and I would fall out, perhaps, in more than one respect; but particularly I would differ with him in this: It does not follow that because a subject may be within the subject matters with which -this Parliament may deal, looking at it from a Dominion point of view, that the province has no power to deal with that same thing, dealing with it from the local or provincial point of view. With regard to this specific matter of prohibition, the judges are on record as maintaining the Canada Temperance Act, and therefore this Parliament has prohibitory legislative power; and as maintaining at the same time the Manitoba and Ontario Provincial Prohibition Acts, so that the provinces have the power of prohibition;-in effect holding that there is a	power	in	either this	Parliamentor a Provincial Parliament to deal with the subject. The case where the Dominion, alone would have the power is	where	the	matter is	dealt withas	one of	Dominion	concernlegislation directed against what is looked upon as a national evil. But, so long as Parliament does not look at it and deal with it in that way, the provincial legislature has the power, dealing with it as a local or provincial evil, to enact legislation for its abatement. Now, as regards the question of manufacture, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair) says it is perfectly clear that the province has no power to absolutely forbid it. I do not undertake to define the exact limit of the power of the provinces to prohibit the manufacture, but I say there is a measure of such power in the provincial legislature. That, I say, repeating, not the words but cer-
tainly the sense of the words, of their Lordships of the Privy Council. If the exigencies of the local law for the abatement of the use-observe the word-of liquor, in order to remove a local or provincial evil, should necessitate the disappearance of the manufacturing, my own personal opinion is that the legislature, dealing with the question from that point of view and for that purpose, could deal with the manufacture. As I have said I do not want to fix the precise line or measure of that power; but, whatever it may be, it has not as yet been exercised by any province. When a province has chosen to do that, then will be time for us to consider two questions,-first, whether any supplementary or ancillary legislation is needed to make it effective, and second, whether it is a proper thing for this Parliament to do in view of what I have .pointed out, that this Parliament, exercising that power, doing that thing, would be doing it in the exercise of its own power of direct prohibition; and I think a serious question would arise as to whether we should exercise this direct power if we exercise it otherwise than in such a manner as to make our law effective throughout the Dominion. I am not saying it could not be done. But I leave it to the people who believe that the measure now before the House is at all events a useful measure, a progressive measure, one that will have its own uses even if you choose to describe it as within a limited field, to say whether it would be wise for us by seeking to graft upon it legislation which, perhaps, may1 be of doubtful validity, to expose the entire measure to being defeated. Let us have this measure, then. It is a good measure; it will give effective assistance. Assume, for the moment, that it zs not .all that this Parliament could do. I do not believe that the Government of any province in Canada believe they have the power to prohibit the manufacture oif liquor and beer within, their province. If the provinces adopting a prohibitory law in respect of the sale of intoxicating liquor within their bounds felt or knew that at the same time they could prohibit the manufacture of liquor within their bounds, they would do so. The reason why they do not prohibit the manufacture is because they feel that they have no power so to prohibit. I venture to say that if any

province had prohibited the manufacture of beer or liquor within its bounds, the legislation so prohibiting would be set at naught because of the fact that only the Dominion Government has the power to deal with importation and manufacture. My hon. friend realizes that, because he has come forward with a Bill designed to assist in preventing importation into the provinces, but leaving out altogether the question of manufacture. Any province seeking to do away with the liquor evil proceeds to do away with the sale. According to the argument of my hon. friend, we shall now be able to stop the importation, but not the manufacture. You cannot have a satisfactory prohibitory law in any province within which the manufacture of liquors is permitted. That has been the one great objection to all provincial and county laws up to the present time. If this Government want to adopt a law that will be of any service to the provinces that have adopted prohibition they should make that law apply just as much to the manufacture of liquor within the bounds of the province as to its importation into the province.

Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew): It has been the practice of the Minister of Railways, on going into committee for the first time, to make a somewhat lengthy statement of the work of the department for the year. We are all very sorry that the minister himself is absent from the House through illness, and we trust that his illness may be of short duration, and that he will be able to return to his place in the department and the Government within a very short time. I wish to make a few observations generally on the work of the department before we proceed to discuss in detail some of the items. I do not intend to go over the whole realm of discussion of the Transcontinental railway; some of us have done that at length at other times. But from what has come to my ears during the past three months, I feel confident that one of the
reasons why there has been a disagreement between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Government lies in the ambition of the general manager of the Government railways to become the head, as manager, of a transcontinental railway. I say that advisedly from what I have heard during the past two or three months. From the time that Mr. Gutelius was called into advise the Government, there have been things done and things left undone to. give the company a reason for not taking over the road. I am not going to discuss whether they were large things or small things; but certain things in the contract, on the advice of Mr. Gutelius, were departed from, notwithstanding the fact that the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway had stated positively that if that course were taken he would not take over the road. But these changes were made just the same. I would go so far as to say that . it is possible the Government did not fully understand the situation in this respect at the time.
At Quebec changes were made without. even the semblance of consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Enormous expenditures were made and there were alterations of. the whole plan, of the terminal facilities and entrance at Quebec. These alone would be full reason why the company could not take over the line without, I believe, going to its shareholders and getting authority to make a new contract or to deviate from the old contract on which they had financed and made all their calculations. In addition to that, I submit to the committee that the changes made at Quebec, so far as the road is concerned, are absolutely wrong and detrimental to it as a transcontinental line, and altogether subversive of the object for which it is being constructed, so far as the port of Quebec is concerned The previous Government, after several consultations with the city of Quebec, the Grand Trunk Pacific and some other railway companies, the Public Works Department and the Department of Marine and Fisheries, had arranged for certain things to be done at Quebec.
A line had been contracted for by the old Quebec Bridge Company to run from the main line just north of the bridge to a point in Quebec at Champlain market. The Transcontinental Commission took that contract over from the Bridge Company and proceeded to build that line. We had arranged for a handsome station at what ' is known as the Champlain market, and we made arrangements, after some difli-

culty, with the city of Quebec to secure certain properties in that vicinity. Just in the locality is a magnificent site for deep water terminals, conveniently situated in the very heart of the trading section of the city. To these conditions, and to that proposition, all parties agreed. Under the Government of which I was a member, shops were to be constructed on the main line at the north end of the bridge. Any person, who knows anything about railway operation, will agree that the less hauling you have of any material for which you get no pay, the better it is. With the shops on the main line, the " lame ducks," as railway men call the cars that are injured or broken in any way, could be shunted and repaired without any expense whatever, so far as hauling is concerned.
Acting on the advice of somebody, the new commission decided that they would not-have the shops on the main line of the system for which they were to be constructed, and so, these shops, which are expensive, have been constructed six miles from the main line. In ordeT to reach these -shops so situated, the Government had either to build a new railway, buy one of the existing lines from the Canadian Pacific railway or Canadian Northern railway, or get running rights. They proceeded to purchase from the Canadian Northern railway, about six miles of road, and to-day the Government owns these six miles of railway, and has to upkeep and maintain them, so that the Canadian Northern is relieved of the expense of keeping up this line to get at the shops. That is not the most serious feature of placing these shops away from the main line. If a thousand cars have to be repaired, say in a year, that means the expense of hauling one oar 12,000 milee, which, -as any railway man can figure out, would amount to quite a sum. Every dollar that is added to the expenses of the road means that much additional cost on the transportation of the goods of the people of Canada. I submit that it is no good to the city of Quebec, particularly, to have the shops down there, or at all events, no more good than if they had been placed where it was originally intended they should be placed.- 'Certainly the location is not so 'beneficial to the line itself. Then these expensive shops have 'been constructed, hut there is no machinery in them. I admiit that at the present time the expenditure of money has to be carefully guarded, and at this moment perhaps, in

the position in which it finds itself, the Government is perhaps justified in being careful, but there was no justification for not going on with the construction of the shops where they were intended to be located. They would have been completed long before the outbreak of the war had not the whole original scheme been abandoned for some reason, which I have never yet heard explained satisfactorily, and to which the people of Quebec, I believe, object. There was to be a goods station-and this was part of the arrangement with the city and with the -Grand Trunk Pacific under the contract-erected on the 'site of the Champlain market, which is right on the river front. That would have been in keeping with the Chateau Frontenac and with the great city of Quebec, and with the traffic that was expected to be through traffic east and west of that city. A small building has been put up o-n the Champlain market, and an arrangement has been entered inlto with the 'Canadian Pacific Railway for the construction of a union station, but that arrangement means that the passenger traffic will not tgo straight down, as was originally intended, but will go away around, following the St. Charles river [DOT] until it enters the Canadian Pacific Railway station. I have asked for -the correspondence time and again, and I think I have seen it all, and it shows th-at the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company would not agree to that. The arrangement was however gone on with. The Grand Trunk Pacific could not agree to it, because there was no -provision that the parent company, the Grand Trunk, could have on any terms the joint use, with the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific Railway, of the Union station. The effect of that would be that if the Grand Trunk Company, which has guaranteed the bonds of a great portion of the Grand Trunk Pacific, ran a through train from Montreal to the Quebec bridge and into the city of Quebec, it could not run into the Union station.
