Wiry not?

The Grand Trunk trains never go over that track, because there is no Quebec bridge and no union station. But in the agreement the Grand Trunk was not included, and was not allowed to use the Canadian Pacific railway line. To my mind the agreement was so absolutely indefensible, from a traffic standpoint, that the Grand Trunk Pacific could not for a

moment think of consenting to it, and the Canadian Pacific railway knew that well.
The situation in Quebec at the present time is that, practically speaking, they might just as well have never heard of the Transcontinental railway. They have a -small station at the Champlain market, and they have practically no freight sheds? and no deep water terminals. For any traffic that may come to Quebec, expecting to be transhipped, there is at the present time absolutely no provision, any more than there was before the Transcontinental was thought of. The Board of Trade of Quebec city absolutely agrees, as I shall show in a few moments, with what I am now placing before the committee. In order to get over this long haul to the Union Station by the St. Charles river, putting Quebec on -a side line, instead; of on the main line of the Transcontinental, it was arranged that a tunnel should be constructed to run from a point on the line that runs from the north end of the bridge to Champlain market, through -and under the city, to the Canadian Pacific railway new station. I have my doubts whether that tunnel will ever 'be constructed. The people of Quebec think at t'he present time that the Government has abandoned the idea of its construction, and, from what I heard in the discussion of the matter in this House last session, I have also come to that conclusion. The Prime Minister went to Quebec and prpmised the people that this tunnel would be constructed. But nothing has been done, and Quebec is really up in arms over the treatment that has been given that city in so far as the Transcontinental railway and its terminals are concerned. All this has cost more money than the old scheme would have cost, and it will cost millions of dollars more than the old scheme before it is through. If we capitalize what the Government have to pay the Canadian Pacific for the joint use of the station, and put in the cost of the new shops, the buying of new land, the buying of a piece of line from the Canadian Northern, and the cost of the train haul away around by the St. Charles, we find that the cost of construction and operation will be a great deal more than it would have been under the original contract. I have been over the territory, whether the acting minister has or not, I know the ground and I have a bird's eye view in my mind of the whole situation. The original scheme was not arrived at without a good deal of consideration and examination. All those suggestions that were made to the
old Government and rejected were made to the new Government and accepted, though a large amount of money had been invested in the former scheme, which investment will to a large extent now be valueless. Nobody is suited by the arrangement in Quebec, and it has cost the people of Canada a lot of money. No benefit comes to the city of Quebec, but injury is done to the transportation problem as a whole. Let me show to the committee what the Board of Trade of Quebec thinks of the situation.
I have here the report of the annual meeting of the Quebec Board of Trade:
Annual Meeting of the Quebec Board of Trade, Feb. 22, 1916.
President's Address.
I shall just read a few extracts from the report. At page 2 the president says:
We have pointed out to the Government that the present entrance from the bridge to the city is not satisfactory, as it involves a detour by Cap Rouge, making the distance over eleven miles, whereas the distance from the bridge to the Champlain market is only about six- miles. This should be remedied, either by making the proposed tunnel from Wolfe's Cove to St. Malo, or by giving suitable terminal accommodation for the south shore roads at the Champlain
market____A few weeks ago, without any
warning and without consulting our commercial men who furnish the traffic, the authorities of the Intercolonial have thought proper to change this system and to send their goods to the Canadian Pacific railway station at the Palais, an unnecessary detour via Cap Rouge of sixteen miles, using the steamer Leonard for the purpose of crossing the river... . Though by no means ,a large or costly edifice, as compared with those built or being built in other cities as union stations, it will no doubt be sufficient for these two roads. No decision seems yet to have been arrived at as to a station for the south shore roads to use, after the completion of the bridge.
That larger scheme, which had been discussed before with the old Government, was simply wiped out, with the result that Quebec is in the situation that I have described. My words have not been really too strong, as my hon. friend will find by reading the address of the president and the report of the Board of Trade. Just let me give another paragraph or two. On page 8 of the president's address, he says:
Of what use was it for Canada to have built three transcontinental railways, at enormous cost, if we have not facilities at our seaports to handle the goods they bring there? The necessity of this was foreseen when the city of Quebec signed a contract with the Commissioners of the Transcontinental railway on the 20th August, 1910, by which in consideration of the transfer by the city of the valuable Champlain market property, at a nominal figure, the Government were to build docks, dock frontage, storage facilities, and terminals on the St. Lawrence front, in Champlain Ward, to the

value of three millions of dollars, exclusive of the cost of right of way and of the workshops. To obtain these concessions, for which the city should not have been called upon to make any sacrifices-other cities were not-the city of Quebec has had to give property and undertake expenditures, which the official report of the city printed in our annual report, estimates at over three millions of dollars, a vast sum, which, this small city can ill afford to contribute at the present time. Subsequent agreements with the Government, as to the use of a union passenger station and the change of location for the Workshops, have not waived in any way our1 right to these freight and shipping terminals, and yet nothing whatever has been done towards them and without them this railway is going to be of very little use to us or to the country. A deputation of your board had an interview with the Prime Minister on this subject, in Ottawa, on the 22nd June last and pointing out to him this alarming position, suggested that the three docks and basins, west of Lampson's Cove, originally recommended by the engineers' joint report of 1906 as freight terminals for this railway, together with grain ' storage for ten millions bushels should be put in at once, and that the 1,800 feet of deep water dock frontage between I.ampson's Cove and the Champlain market, which was under contract when the city signed its agreement with the Government Commissioners in 1910 should also be completed. Sir Robert Borden assured us that he quite understood the necessity of proper facilities for the freight traffic of the transcontinental, but that the war had interfered with, financial matters to such an extent that at Halifax, where a vast plan of similar terminals was under contract, they had been obliged to limit the work for the present, to one unit out of six. Nevertheless he said he appreciated the importance of keeping Canadian trade in Canadian channels and he would certainly do, under the circumstances, all that he could to fulfil his duty.
The Board of Trade winds up by saying that it is the Government's duty to announce what they propose to do with this terminal, even if at the present moment conditions are such that the work cannot be proceeded with. I want to add that if no change had been made in the scheme, which change had injured it very materially from the transportation point of view, the delay would not have occurred, and much of this work would have been done before there was any war. The president says further:
The great sacrifices which the city of Quebec is making for them should entitle us to this. Unless we are going to get what was agreed upon, it seems to me that it would be much wiser for the city of Quebec to cancel - the arrangements for a union station with the Canadian Pacific railway and revert to the position we held under the agreement of August 20, 1910.
Take the report of the Quebec Board of Trade itself, which contains some of the correspondence.
 ,
I thought my hon. friend was reading from the report of the Quebec Board of Trade.

No, I was reading from the annual address of the president of the Quebec Board of Trade. The report of the Quebec Board of Trade, which, by the way, is a very interesting document, gives a lot of material concerning the facilities of that port. The documents from which I am going to quote have a direct bearing on this question. A good deal of correspondence took place between the Quebec Board of Trade, its officials, and the Government. Here is the report of the annual meetiug of the Quebec Board of Trade:
At a meeting of the council held on the 26th day of March (1915) among the correspondence read were letters from Hon. T. Chase Casgrain, Postmaster General, giving some particulars about the public works to be continued in the port of Quebec. , In the last letter he said: " You may be sure it is the Government's intention to push work for the handling of the Transcontinental railway during the summer months. Both the passenger stations will go on, as will also the work of the Harbour Commission, the damming of the St. Charles river and the Graving dock at Lauzon. The amount voted for the Transcontinental at all points between Winnipeg and Moncton, is $5,000,000 and $3,500,000 to continue work on the bridge."
As the council desired to secure more particulars about terminals the secretary was directed to write the Postmaster General concerning them.
Certain resolutions in reference to trade, freight rates, etc., were passed by the board and copies sent to the different Boards of Trade in Canada, as far west as the Pacific, I think. I should like to quote from a letter written to the Postmaster General. A letter was also written to the Minister of Railways, covering about the same ground, but touching on other matters as well. On page 230 of this report we find some correspondence from the Quebec B-oarid of Trade to the minister representing them in the Cabinet, as follows:
When the Government or the Transcontinental authorities came to the decision to make use of a union station with the Canadian Pacific railway at the Palais, instead of the large maritime station then under contract at the Champlain market, many business men doubted the wisdom of the changebut as it was then well understood that the freight business of the road would be done on the St. Lawrence front, and as the Government have since erected a building on the Champlain market site for that purpose, the question of passenger business being considered of minor importance, no objection was raised to a union passenger station. But this new departure of the Intercolonial authorities, as to the ferry and as to removal of the freight from the water front, reopens the whole question of railway terminals at Quebec, and this question is so important for us, that

I hope you will pardon me if I give you the following summary of the views of our commercial men on the subject;
1.	The Union station is not a Union station unless the passenger trains of all south shore roads can and will come into it. If it is restricted to the use of the Canadian Pacific railway and the Tran scon: mental, of what use will it be to the city when the bridge is built? If it is open to the use of the south shore roads upon what terms can they use it? The Grand Trunk and the Delaware and Hudson have asked us this question, and we cannot tell them. Is there any agreement signed between the Government and the Canadian Pacific railway for the use and operation of this station? Even if the south shore roads are to be admitted, it is certain that they will not come to the Palais via Cap Rouge, a distance of 11 miles from the north end of the bridge, when the distance to the Champlain Market is only 6 miles.

Why can not they use the
Champlain Market station now?

The building was only
erected a short time ago.
The tracks are there.

There is not accommodation for more than one road. The idea of making it a terminal has been abandoned. No one would think of using that as a joint station. There are no railway facilities around to handle the traffic, and there is only one small building, which the people of Quebec call " The Match-Box." The report goes on:
The only way to bring them to the Union station will be to build the tunnel from Wolfe's Cove to St. Malo, and even this will only reduce the distance to 8.03 miles. If there is to be no tunnel, it would be better to abandon the idea of a union station at the Palais, and revert to the original plan of a maritime station at the Champlain market, similar to that being built at Halifax. This would relieve the city of Quebec of some of the heavy obligations it has undertaken.
.We are still strongly of the opinion that all the freight business of the Transcontinental railway should be done on the St. Lawrence front; that docks and elevators should be built between Lampsons' Cove and Wolfes' Cove, and that a deep water sea wall should be built between Lampsons' and the Champlain market which would not only do away with the disgraceful appearance of the railway approach to the city, but would give the railway valuable property and steamship berths on the deep water frontage. All these things were to have been done by the former Transcontinental Commission, and that was the consideration for which the city gave away the valuable Champlain market property for a nominal price.
Another clause reads:
The wholesale trade complain very much of the removal of the freight business of the Intercolonial railway to the Palais, and say that their cartage costs them 50 per cent more than at any other place, besides greater delay in handling.
I could read a great deal more, but I think I have read enough to show that the Board of Trade, representing the citizens of Quebec, absolutely concurs in the view I have placed before the committee, that the new scheme is not as good for the city of Quebec; it is not as good for the business men, and will add very materially to the cost of handling all traffic that goes into the city. As a matter of fact, as regards both passengers and freight, it will place Quebec several miles further away from the Transcontinental than it was under the previous arrangement.
At Halifax enormous sums of money are being expended, running into many, many millions of dollars. Undoubtedly it is necessary to expend a large sum of money on our ocean ports; but did the Government go about this matter as business men would have done who were trying to make a success of transportation? The terminal facilities in contemplation at Halifax are far and away in execess of the hauling capacity of the railway to Halifax. Let me explain what I mean. All the way from Moncton to Halifax there is but one line of railway-the Intercolonial. Goods that go by rail to Halifax, whether belonging to the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Intercolonial, must go over that one line of track. Now, to provide for very, very adequate terminals without making preparations for the haulage of a sufficient quantity of goods to occupy those terminals, would not be considered good business by railway companies. If the terminals at Halifax are necessary-and I am not disputing that for the moment-it is, and has been, absolutely necessary that at least a double track, or perhaps a track through another section of the country, should be constructed from Moncton to Halifax in order to carry the traffic. This is not a new matter; it has been discussed for many years; in fact, from the moment the large terminal facilities were started at Halifax. I submit that the added ability, so to speak, of the railway to carry this expected increase in traffic should have been made simultaneously with the building of the terminals. I do not know that I want to discuss that phase any further, although I have a good many things before me concerning it.
Let me now turn to operation. I say without fear of contradiction that whatever the design may have been, the result of the operation of the Transcontinental has been to make that road, east of Cochrane^ value-

less. A cheap homeseekers' excursion, I am told, is run on the Intercolonial railway from the Maritime Provinces. If I am wrong in this I wish to be corrected. I am told that that excursion did not use the Transcontinental railway as it ought (to do. The .train runs to Montreal, and .there the traffic is given-to the Grand Trunk and goes thence by the Grand Trunk through to North Bay, then by the Ontario Government railway to join the Transcontinental, entirely ignoring thev Transcontinental from Quebec city through to Cochrane. It may be argued that that was done in order to pick up traffic along the road. There can be no other .reason, and if that .is not the reason the manager of the Intercolonial railway, if he arranged, that through homeseekers' excursion, has no business to take our traffic and give the big share of the profits to the Grand Trunk railway. The minister tells us that the Intercolonial has done wonderfully well in the past year. I am convinced that no effort is being made, so far as operation is concerned, to give the Transcontinental east of Cochrane the faintest ghost of a chance. Is my hon.' friend sure that goods coming into Quebec from the West are not handed over to the Intercolonial to swell the traffic of that road, instead of being sent through to Moncton on the Transcontinental? It is the easiest thing in the world, when two Toads have the same management, to hand the traffic over from one road to the other .so that the receipts of the one will be swelled immensely and the receipts of the other made practically nil. An^ is it not true that traffic originating in the Maritime Provinces and destined for the West is carried over the Intercolonial? Does this not explain in part why the Intercolonial is congested, and why we are told that it has not power enough, or not enough cars, so that there is complaint of congestion along that line, while the Transcontinental is scarcely running a train? The Transcontinental could take a laTge share of that freight, and avoid the congestion. The minister may say that we have not the oaTS, but why have not the cars been secured to handle a fair amount of traffic on the Transcontinental? I am afraid, from the information that has come to me within the past few weeks from certain shippers, that their goods have been crowded on the Intercolonial when they might have been handled expeditiously and conveniently on the Transcontinental, and that traffic has been handed to the Inter-[Alr. Graham.]
colonial that should not have gone on that road at all until it reached Moncton.
The operation of the Transcontinental east of Cochrane is no operation at all; that is it is not what railway men would call operation. My hon. friend said the other night that up to date it had paid its way. Well, if the road can pay its way with the abortive operation that has been given it, it might do far better if it had any kind of a fair chance. We find that there is only an occasional passenger train run over the line, and when I say passenger train, I mean a real passenger train. That is no way to develop trade over a railroad; that is no way to bring a railroad before the public. If I am rightly informed as to the kind of management there has been, and if that kind of management is to continue the Transcontinental east of Cochrane cannot help but be a failure. There may be some reason for a more irregular traffic east of Cochrane to some points than there is west; but I submit to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Marine, that the Transcontinental east of Quebec is not being used for the convenience of the people as it should be, but is kept practically closed, while the Intercolonial is said to be congested. Every time a complaint is made as to lack of accommodation on the Intercolonial, the answer is sent from Moncton: we are doing the best we can, but the traffic is congested. We have two roads, and there is no reason why traffic should be congested unless there is neglect in the getting the rolling stock necessary to move the traffic, or unless the line is being misused, for what purpose I know not.
For what purpose was the Transcontinental constructed? We all agree that one object was to develop the ocean ports of Canada. At the present moment not one practical step is being taken to bring the traffic to these ocean ports over the Transcontinental.
We find that a fast train is run tri-weekly from the city of Toronto through to the city of Winnipeg, over the Grand Trunk, the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario, and the Transcontinental, whilst east of Cochrane the people hardly know that there is a Transcontinental railway though they have paid their share of the money to construct it. If it is argued that the line does not pay at the present time, let me tell the minister that his manager does not know whether it will pay or not because he has not given it a trial. Many .railways in Canada have been run for two or three

years at a loss, and yet the Board of Railway Commissioners would compel them to operate if they attempted to cease operating, and the law very properly gives the Railway Commissioners that power because there is something above the making of profits, and that is the accommodation of the people. The people east of Cochrane, so far as the Transcontinental is concerned, are not being accommodated, though _ they have in it the same investment per capita of population as have the people west of Cochrane, or as have the people of any portion of the Dominion. I have been in the province of Quebec more or less and have heard a good many complaints which I am laying before the minister in as practical a way as I can. I say that it iis the duty of the Government to see to it that the manager of the Government railways makes at least an experiment in the operation of the Transcontinental east of Cochrane. On the road running from Toronto 'to the West via Cochrane, it is advertised by this Government that the Transcontinental is the last word in the perfection of railway construction. I am glad that they think that now. But the railway east of Cochrane to the city of Quebec is just as good as a railway as it is west of Cochrane, and, except for ope or two pusher grades, the Tailway 'from Quebec to Moncton has no equal on the continent of America. And yet, for some reason, it is left to-day practically unused, for fear that for the time being it will not pay. I say it is the duty of the Government, no matter what the manager may think, to give the operation of this portion of the Toad a fair trial. During the past few months, the income of other railways has increased at a very rapid rate, and I believe that if the railway east of Cochrane had been operated for the accommodation of the people, even to a somewhat limited extent, the result would have been quite surprising to the Government and to the manager. We have said in this House -and the Prime Ministers of Ontario and Quebec have said it also-that' along the line of the Transcontinental railway east of Cochrane there is much valuable terri. tory to be developed. If the railway, for which the people have paid, is not made the means of affording them an opportunity to go to that territory, it will remain as unexplored and undeveloped, as if there had been no Tailway.
One great means of progress for the hinterland of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec would be the operation of that railway from Cochrane east to the city of Quebec and a fairly good operation from Quebec east. If we are not going to use the line east of Cochrane; if the Government is going to stop at that terminal and hand the traffic that goes east over to the Grand Trunk Pacific to go by Scotia Junction and over the Grand Trunk line to Montreal; if that is to be the settled policy, what is to become of Quebec, Halifax and St. -John as ocean terminals? If that is to be done, these ports might as well have no increased terminal facilities; the spending of all this money will be of no use. Sir, the time has confe when the Government must take a hand in the management of this road. They should advise its manager that the Trancontinental was built for the purpose of carrying the goods of the people, not only to Cochrane, but all the way from the city of Winnipeg to the city of Moncton. If the Grand Trunk Pacific railway had had the road, the Board of Railway Commissioners would have compelled them to operate that portion of the line. The Government of Canada is setting a mighty bad example by giving a poorer service to the people who paid for the road and who own it than they would require from a company which had spent its own money in constructing the road.
Let me refer for two or three minutes to the question of the Trent canal. I have a good many familiar documents here, though perhaps they are not so familiar to this Government as they are to me. I think it is fair that somefone should set forth the position of Federal authority with reference to the Trent Valley water-power. If has been intimated that the Dominion Government were interlopers on that territory so far as power development was concerned. Originally the water-powers along the Trent system were divided into very small entities or units. Some of the patents go back over a hundred years; there was a diversity of patents in respect of little water-powers owned by certain individuals. When there was a plentiful supply of timber in the Trent valley, the Provincial Government of Ontario had the rights in the dams, in many of the lakes and waters generally along that system. When the supply of timber became nearly exhausted the Ontario Government found that the upkeep of these dams and locks was very expensive, and they wished to be relieved of the expense of that upkeep. The expense to the Ontario Government, if I

remember correctly, was about $20,000 a year. As long as the dues from lumbermen were received the upkeep of these dams was a paying investment, but when the timber supply was exhausted it was a case of an outlay without any in-9 p.m. come. When the construction of the Trent canal was being proceeded with, the Federal authorities found that they needed all these waters for the purposes of navigation, and that in the further development of them and in the construction of the canal, further water poweT would of necessity result. The correspondence began in 1904, when Mr. Justice Latohford was Commissioner of Public Works for Ontario, and Mr. Campbell, the present Deputy Minister of Railways at Ottawa was Deputy Commissioner of Public Works at Toronto. Mr. Campbell made a Teport to his chief, the Commissioner of Public Works, on March 1, 1904, in which he set out the cost of maintain-enee of these dams and suggested what ought to he included in any agreement made for their transference to the Dominion. I think I can make it clear that *the Ontario Government handed these over of their own free will by Order in Council to the Federal authority without any compensation whatever and without retaining for themselves any right they might have in provincial water powers. Mr. Campbell, in this first report that he made to the commissioner, said:
That the transfer of these locks, dams and other works does in no way prejudice or interfere with provincial rights upon or adjacent to . any streams, lakes or other waters affected, as regards water-powers, which it may hereafter be desirable to utilize, navigation to be aided, Crown lands to be flooded, mines to be developed, or other valuable privilege.
Would it not be well to quote the report agreed upon by the two Governments in 1905 and 1906?

It will be quoted to the satisfaction-well, maybe not to the satisfaction of my hon. friend, but at any rate to the extent of substantiating what I am saying. I am pointing out that the then Deputy Commissioner of Public Works in Ontario impressed on his Government the necessity of having a clause put in the agreement providing that there should be retained to the province all the rights that they might have in these water powers. 1 find that Mr. Jones, secretary of the Department of Railways and Canals, wrote in reply to this memorandum, which no doubt was sent to Ottawa, a letter in which he

refers to this very section which I have read. Of course, his reference to it would mean a reference to it by the Department of .Railways. He said: [DOT]
Section 4 should be more fully explained as the terms seem to be ambiguous. As regards any water-powers that are at the dams, 1 should think they should go with the dams. If the Dominion Government are to he hampered by the consideration of water users at the several dams, as they surely would he when the waters above the dams would be drawn down to the lowest possible level, the usefulness of the reservoirs would be very much impaired, and the object for which the transfer is to be made would he defeated. The same remark might apply to the reference "Navigation to he aided."
That has reference, as will be observed, to the clause which I read regarding the retention by the Ontario Government of their rights in respect of water-powers. I find a letter from H. H. Hansard, law clerk of the Department of Railways and Canals, to which these matters were referred in September, 1914. I wish to read the clauses referring to the question which has been so much discussed:
As to guaranteeing to existing owners or lessees of water-powers derived from or depending on any of the present dams, etc.
The continuance of such existing rights to he guaranteed, or compensation to he paid therefor in the usual manner.
Provincial rights, however, to water-powers derived from or depending on any of the same dams to be transferred to the Dominion and no guarantee or compensation to be given in respect thereof.
I am calling attention to this to show that the matter was fully discussed, pro and con, before a decision was arrived at. I find a letter from Richard B. Rogers, superintending engineer of the Trent canal, dated December 7, 1904, and written to Mr. Collingwood Schreiber.
Sir Collingwood Schreiber.

Mr. Collingwood Schreiber then; Sir Collingwood Schreiber now.
With reference to water-powers at the dams to be handed over, or hereafter to he constructed, Jhe assistant commissioner objected to the wording of the statement made in the report of our last interview by Mr. Hansard, in section 3 of such report, namely:	" Such
right to be transferred." He contended that if the dams were handed over to the Dominion Government, or new dams were constructed by the Dominion Government, that the Ontario Government would have no water-power rights at these dams, and therefore it was unnecessary to refer to " The rights being transferred." The same reference to transferring water-powers is made also in sectidn 9 of said report. If such is the contention I see no reason why this omission should not be made.

That is, it was decided that if the dams went the water powers would go as a matter of course, and there was no need of mentioning rights, so they did not mention them at all, it being understood between them that when the dams went the right to water powers went with them. I find a letter from Mr. Alward, assistant law clerk of the department, dated the 7th of December, 1904, in which he deals with the matter in this way:
That the proposed transfer of dams and rights to construct or reconstruct, maintain and operate dams on the said water shall include the transfer of provincial rights to and in water-powers only at the point of such dams that now exist or that may hereafter exist; and the rights to operate any such dam. ...
He was of the opinion that it would be well to put in a clause stating in so many words that they were not transferred.
I wish to refer to the Order in Council of the Ontario Government, dated the 22nd of July, 1905. I call the attention of the committee to the fact that in the meantime the Government of Ontario had changed, and the Conservative Government, of which my friend, Sir Adam Beck, was a member, came into office before this transfer took place. In July, 1905, an Order in Council was passed by the present Ontario Government, and I propose to read this Order in Council, so that there can be no mistake about it, because I think the Federal authority has been criticised unduly for its handling of these water powers. As a matter of fact, these dams and lakes were given over voluntarily to the Dominion, and the Ontario Government was glad to get rid of them in order to avoid expense. The Order in Council of the Conservative Government of Ontario, which has since been reor-ganizecj, is dated July 22, 1905, and is as follows:
Upon consideration of the report of the Hon. the Commissioner of Public Works, dated 15th May, 1905, the Committee of Council advise that certain dams, canals, and other works on waters tributary to the Trent Valley canal heretofore constructed and maintained by the Department of Public Works, Ontario, be transferred to the Department of Railways and Canals, Canada, upon the following terms, in order that the said waters and works may be regulated for the purposes of the said Trent Valley canal:
1.	That all the locks, dams, rights in waters and flooded lands and other works as shown by the hereto attached list and plan be transferred to the Dominion Government represented by the Department of Railways and Canals free of all cost.
2.	That the Dominion Government shall assume, operate and keep in good repair and condition for all time, the lock and three swing
bridges at Lindsay, the lock at Balsam river, and the lock and swing bridge at Yonge'8 Point, together with all minor works in connection with the maintenance and operation of the locks and bridges at Lindsay, Balsam river and Yonge's Point, relieving the province from all expense and responsibility in connection therewith.
3.	That the right of reservoir construction by the Dominion Government shalj be exercisable on and limited to the following: Gull river, Burnt river, Squaw river, Nogies creek. Deer bay, Mississauga creek, Eel's creek and Jack's creek and the drainage areas of such rivers and creeks.
4.	That the following dams shall he maintained for all time by the Dominion Government, subject as hereinafter provided:
On Gull river waters: Balsam lake, Gull lake, Horseshoe lake, Hawk lake. Paint lake, Hall's lake, Keneeris lake, Redstone lake, Eagle and Moose lake, Oblong and Haliburton lake, Percy lake.
On Burnt river waters: Kocklong lake, Drag lake, Loon lake, Big Bear lake, Otter lake, Grace lake, Farquar lake.
On Noggies creek: Swamp lake.
On Mississauga creek: Gull lake, Eagle lake.
5.	That with regard to the smaller or other dams not being actually required by the department for the proposed reservoir system, but now utilized for the flotation of logs, the Dominion Government shall not be required to maintain these dams except only for so long as they are of material use for the purpose of log flotation or log navigation.
6.	That the Dominion will pay to the province at the rate of 50 cents per acre for all unpatented provincial lands flooded through the construction of the proposed reservoir; that compensation for the flooding of patented lands and for damage done to timber on patented lands or on unpatented lands under license to lumberman and others he a matter of agreement between the Dominion Government and the owners or licensees of such lands or timber, and in the event of failure of such owners or licensees to agree with the Dominion Government regarding such compensation, then the matter shall he left to the determination of the Exchequer .Court of Canada in the usual manner.
7.	That the Minister of Railways and Canals shall have the right at any time to rebuild and maintain dams at present existing or at any time to construct and maintain dams in lieu thereof, at other than the present sites for the same; to increase or decrease the heights of all or any of such dams; to determine the size and capacity of the openings therein and the means of controlling the water supply thereat, and to construct or reconstruct, operate and maintain the works necessary to the same, also from time to time to build and maintain new dams wherever he may deem advisable for the proper carrying out of proposed reservoir system, and to maintain and operate the same.
8.	That all mines and minerals in unpatented provincial lands taken over and flooded in th/.i course of construction of reservoirs be reserved to the province, and that all mines and minerals on unpatented lands are still to remain the property of the patentee until proper compensation he granted therefor, and all reasonable provisions essential to the operation and working of the same be allowed subject to the requirements of navigation of the Trent canal.
9.	That the Dominion Government guarantees



to the owners and lessees of timber lands tributary to the streams and lakes affected by this ' Order and to lumbermen now or hereafter operating on such streams and lakes all rights they at present enjoy or are entitled to, by any law or statute now in force with regard to the use and enjoyment of rivers and streams, and also guarantees to the owners and lessees from time to time on any waater power derived from such lakes and streams all rights they at present enjoy or are entitled to by virtue of any law or statute now in force, and in the event of such rights being injuriously affected by the action of the Dominion Government their successors, assigns, employees or representatives in connection with such waters and streams, then the owners and lessees of such timber lands, timber and water power shall have the right to submit their claims to the Exchequer Court of Canada for adjudication and compensation in the usual manner.
Certified.
Lonsdale Copreol, Clerk, Executive Council.
My reason for reading this document is that I wanted it to go on Hansard, because it will be seen that the entire terms of the transfer are contained in it. It will be seen that the province of Ontario saw to it that the Dominion guaranteed to protect the owners of small water powers which had evidently been granted to them by the Provincial Government, but so far as their own water powers were concerned nothing was said about them. An Order in Council was passed by the Dominion Government on February 16, 1906, which is practically a copy of the Order in Council of the Ontario Government, accepting the terms of the Ontario Government. I think it is but fair to the Federal authority that the country should know that they did not take possession of these lakes, reservoirs and water powers in an arbitrary manner. The present Ontario Government, with Sir Adam Beck as one of its members, passed, an Order in Council in 1905 giving these water reservoirs, dams, and everything connected with them, to the Dominion Government free of all cost, the stipulation that they made being that lands flooded should be paid for by the Dominion Government, and that any small holders of water-powers should have their rights protected by the Federal authority, as they would have been protected by the province. That was, in my opinion, the only reasonable thing for both Governments to do. The Dominion Government could not well go on constructing the canal, depending on the supply of water, and on what the province might do. It was only wisdom that the proprietorship of these waters should be handed over to the authority that was going to build the canal and that needed the 
water, and the Ontario Government did not care to keep on expending $20,000 for the upkeep of dams, from which it received no revenue. Up to that date there was no difference of opinion. As the canal construc-, tion continued, it will be readily understood that a comparatively large development of water powers would necessarily take place, though the construction of the canal was the prime object. Then the water powers, of course, as well as others that were vested, as the federal authority claimed in the Dominion, belonged to the federal authority, as outlined in the Order in Council, and something had to be done in order to utilize these powers.
Had the late Government developed a water-power policy?

I will come to that in a moment. There are two ways of reasoning, and two ways of getting at an object. You know, when a squirrel wants to get to a certain limb of a tree, it goes around the-tree first, but a bird flies straight to the point, and, in like manner, my hon. friend from Peterborough jumps to his conclusions; whereas I feel my way as I go, and in the end we may arrive at the same point. In 1907, when I was called to the Government, I found the condition that I have outlined, and so far as the water-powers were concerned, they had been handed over to the Dominion Government. We were proceeding to construct a canal and to erect dams at the particular places outlined, at which a great amount of extra power was being developed. Arrangements had to be made with every small owner so that he should receive an equivalent in electricity or on water-power for that which he owned when we took possession of his property. I think I am safe in saying that there were scores and scores of such cases. If one looks over the reports of the Hydro-Electric Commission he will see that it was urged-the report on this very Trent canal project was made iby the engineer of the Hydro-Electric, if I remember rightly-and urged with reason, that the only way to get power fairly cheap from the Trent system was to have it combined into one distributing system. A multitude of small powers could not be developed, and, particularly, could not be distributed with any degree of success, so far as the consumer was concerned.
That being the case, after a good many months of consultation, I arranged with certain gentlemen that if they, instead of

us, would undertake to get control of these smaller powers, we would deal with them re one body, instead of dealing with them individually, and we would arrange with them, if satisfactory arrangements could be made, ae they were made, that they should undertake to distribute the power under certain restrictions passed by the Dominion Government. West of Toronto at that time, power was 'being distributed very cheaply, and to the advantage of 'the people, from the development of Niagara by the HydroElectric, and the people of central Ontario were at a great disadvantage in the matter of power. Tihat arrangement was' made, and in order that the rates might be controlled, an amendment was made to the Railway Act 'giving the Board of Railway Commissioners power to settle the price at which electricity should be .sold by this company. Ae I remember, it went further, and gave the Railway Commissioners power to compel the company to supply electricity at any point, even in small quantities, at a price which the commissioners thought was fair. The reason for that was that the objection was raised at the time, that some large companies, having interests at one point, would give that particular point a supply of power at the expense of some other point in which they had no interest, and which could not get the power at the same price. That clause was put in the Act to give the Board of Railway Commissioners power to compel the company to supply power where it was needed, and at a price to be fixed by the commissioners. To that I do not think there was one dissenting voice.
They did not know anything about it then.

It was a fair arrangement. That company went on developing power, and a good many towns have received cheap power since. Certain unforeseen complications arose concerning certain cities, and undoubtedly, there was some reason for their complaint. But, what has happened during the last few weeks? While those other places in central Ontario, had the benefit of cheap power for several years, under the conditions I have named, the time has come when the Hydro-Electric wishes to extend its territory further east. How is that to be accomplished? The only way in which it could be accomplished, and the only fair way, is that which has been adopted. I have heard some criticism of the fact that the Ontario Government stepped in and purchased the Seymour Power Company. I say that that was a reasonable thing to do, and the right thing to do, so long as they did not pay too much for it, and I understand that both parties to the agreement considered it to be a fair arrangement. I know that they got a good plant and a good distributing outfit. No disadvantage is coming to any person as the result of that arrangement, and I commend the Ontario Government for it. The Hydro-Electric is extending its work east of Toronto, and it seems reasonable and fair, and in the interests of the entire public, that the distribution should be in the hands of one central power. So far as I am concerned, I am heartily in favour of the action which the Ontario Government has taken, and I trust that the power users in central Ontario will receive all the benefit possible from the new arrangement. Possibly the overhead expenses can be reduced when the1 distribution is under one central authority. The next thing will be, I suppose, to extend the work still further east and give the people of eastern Ontario the advantage.
I consider that one of the great benefits that has come to the province of Ontario during the past few years has come from the work of the Hydro-Electric Commission. They have given electric powers such as have never been given before, and they have distributed to thp small user as well as the large user. The people west of Toronto, particularly, and those to the east, now that the Commission is extending its work, are receiving a benefit which, I believe, they would never have received under other circumstances.
I wish to ask the minister a question or two before I sit down. We ought to have the terms of the lease of the road from Superior Junction to Lake Superior. We ought to have before us the full expenditure that has been made on Halifax harbour up to date. We ought to have the receipts and expenditures of the line from Superior Junction to Lake Superior since it came under Government control. We ought to have the receipts and expenditures of the new train from Toronto to Winnipeg, or our portion of it at least. We ought to have the number of trains that are run daily or weekly between Cochrane and La Tuque, between La Tuque and Quebec, and over the different sections of the railway east of Quebec, with the receipts and expenditures and the amount of traffic hauled.

Mr. Chairman, I think we may safely say that the resume, or synopsis, which the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) has given of the history of the Trent water-powers, is both fairly clear and reasonable up to a certain point. I believe the ex-minister is a man of very statesmanlike inclinations; that he is thoroughly interested in Canada, as a patriot, and that he desires to do the best he can. But, unfortunately, like the rest of us, he has his limitations, and we must all be judged by our limitations. The history of the Trent water-powers may be truthfully summed up by saying that when that district ceased to be a revenue-producing district to the Ontario Government, they were quite willing to get rid of it to anybody who would take it. The Dominion Government had an interest in it-the interest of navigation. They were then beginning to develop that historic waterway known as the Trent canal. They wanted control over the water, and in 1905 and 1906 the two Governments, the Ontario Government and the Dominion Government, came together and completed the transfer. At that time there appeared to be, and there were, a great many valuable water-powers. Now, I find serious fault with the late Government, with the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, and with his immediate predecessor, in that they did not foresee the necessity of retaining for the people of Canada the ownership of these same water-powers. They had no objection to devise a policy, undoubtedly on the correct principle and of the utmost value in theory to the people of that district, not, however, for the Government of Canada to carry out, but for other people to carry out. Here was a lot of water-power that was soon to be exceedingly valuable to the people, but, strange to say, although it seemed to be an extremely valuable asset to the people, they alienated it for next to nothing. There is where the inexcusable blunder took place. I am not fully acquainted with it. I do not know what took place in the department. The hon. member states that there was a sub-committee formed and that they took this up with Mr. Hays. If he was a member of that sub-committee, he knows whether there were any documents or correspondence connected with it, and if there are I will be very glad to submit them.

I called the attention ol the Minister of Railways and Canals to the proposal that Mr. Hays had made to us. I told him that the late Government were favourable to it, and I asked him if he would take up the subject again with the Grand Trunk Pacific. I understood him to say that he would do so and that he would submit to the House the result of it. Surely, there must be some correspondence upon it.

The hon. member tells the
House there was a sub-committee and that there was an arrangement made.

That was during the
time of the late Government.
Mr.'REID:	Yes. Does the hon. gentleman know if there was anything in writing?

Nothing in writing at
that time.

If there is nothing in writing there is nothing that has changed the situation since that time. If there was anything in writing you could deal with the matter but apparently there was nothing at all. The hon. gentleman knows that there was an understanding between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Government that the road was to be taken over in sections by the Grand Trunk Pacific when it was completed and that it was to he taken over and operated on such conditions as the arbitrator, Sir William Whyte, should determine. The first section between Superior Junction and Winnipeg was taken over in order that the Grand Trunk Pacific might operate between Winnipeg and Fort William going over their own Superior Junction branch. Had an arrangement, such as the hon. gentleman has mentioned, been agreed upon there would have been no necessity for arbitration. The Grand Trunk Pacific never put up any agreement such as that described by the hon. gentleman, but they left it to Sir William Whyte and Sir William Whyte, in his award, said that they would pay so much per annum rental on each section taken over. But they never took over any other portions of the road because they were not completed. The whole road was handed over then at the end of two years. They leased that portion of the road between Winnipeg and Superior Junction for two years. The reason they took a two years lease was that that portion of the road was ready to be operated. But, from Superior Junction east the road was not in a condition to operate trains over and the very minute it was completed, the two years were up, their lease expired, they refused to take over any portion of the Transcontinental railway between Winnipeg and Moncton and the Government have had to operate it.

Before we pass the
Estimates, will the minister bring down that correspondence? I cannot imagine that it is possible, in an important matter like the operation of the Transcontinental railway, that this refusal should be based simply upon a verbal statement. There must be something in writing and this Parliament is entitled to have the correspondence. H the Grand Trunk Pacific have refused to take the road over, Parliament has the right to be informed of the grounds upon which they have refused, the terms
of their refusal and the request which the Government have made to them to operate. That request would he in writing. iSo far this Parliament has no information whatever of a written character but just that the Grand 'Trunk Pacific complained of the degrading of the railway, complained of the alteration in the terminals at Quebec without their consent, and claimed that they were not bound by the contract to undertake the operation until the specifications were carried out in that respect. That is the only written information which this Parliament has and I submit that before these Estimates are passed this Parliament should be informed on the subject and should have the correspondence.
I am particularly concerned, on behalf of my constituency and the Maritime Provinces generally, in the arrangement made between the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific being carried out in good faith and in its entirety. I think that the taking over by the Government of a part of the Transcontinental railway and the attempt to operate it, if there had been a .chance of getting the Grand Trunk Pacific to undertake its operation under a temporary arrangement pending the completion of the line, when they would enter into a lease, is an operation of the most farcical character and one that is not in the interest of the Maritime Provinces or of Canada as a whole. If the Grand Trunk Pacific had undertaken the operation of the road, as they were willing to do, as they offered the late Government to* do, as I believe they have always been willing to do for the present Government, they would be interested in the development of industries, in the increasing of traffic, and in the bringing about of an increased earning power that would be to their own benefit in the future. The Intercolonial railway is not interested in developing industries along that line, and is not interested in doing anything for the future if it is to be handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I charge that upon the railway between Cochrane and Moncton the Government are not giving a service that is worthy of being called a railway service. Between Cochrane and Winnipeg, on an average, it takes about an hour to run 13 miles.
That is fast enough.
And they do not run at night. No encouragement is given to traffic.
There is no traffic.

No effort is made to operate the road as it should be operated. When the Transcontinental was built, it was built under an implied contract between all the provinces of Canada. It was intended to be a transcontinental line, extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific, every mile of which would be on Canadian territory. That was the essence and spirit of the contract. It was provided that traffic originating on the Grand Trunk Pacific in the West should be carried in winter and in summer to Canadian ports. We all knew that the Grand Trunk Pacific was deeply interested in the American port of Portland, in the state of Maine, and the Government stipulated that the Grand Trunk Pacific should carry (its traffic to Canadian ports. Under the terms of the -agreement, it was to the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific that their traffic should be so carried, for they were to operate the eastern division when the road was completed. I do not hesitate to say th-at it was one of the most monstrous and unjustifiable thing-s the Government could have done to go to work and violate the specifications and the terms of the agreement, -so as to make it impossible for the officers of the Grand Trunk Pacific, if they had regard to the interests of their shareholders, to enter on the operation of the road. This Government fa-as so acted by altering the grades and the terminals without the consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific, as to mak-e it the duty, of the officials of that railway company to refuse, in the interests of their shareholders, to enter upon the operation of the line until the specifica

 tions have been lived up to. But as I understand it, the Grand Trunk Pacific have already said to this Government that when the specifications are fulfilled they will be prepared to enter into a lease, and operate the road according to its terms; and until the Minister of Railways denies the truth of what I have said, I shall believe that the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific has told this Government and the present Minister of Railways, just as he told our Government, that pending the completion of the road in accordance with the specifications, they will be- willing to enter on the operation of sections as they are completed, under the terms- I have mentioned as having been submitted by the late president to a committee of the Council of the late Government. ' It is, I am sorry to say, too -much the fashion 
of gentlemen on- the other side of the House to disparage the Transcontinental. Not long .ago the Solicitor General was reported to have referred, in the city of Montreal, to the Transcontinental as simply being two streaks of rust which were of no use to the country, and which remained as a monument to the folly of the late Government.

Hear, hear.
Mr. PU-GSLEY: And gentlemen are found to-night to say " hear, hear." The other night the hon. -member for Lambton- (Mr. Armstrong) said -that the sleepers on the Transcontinental were rotting, and the rails rusting. I ask my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Railways if these statements are true. I ask him if the Transcontinental all the wpy from -the city of Moncton to *the city of Winnipeg is not one of the finest roads on the American continent. He knows there is no 'better road on the American continent to-day than the Transcontinental all the way from the city of Moncton to the city of Winnipeg. We have heard remarks -made before in this House, as well as this session, in disparagement of the Transcontinental. It was my pleasure not long -ago to travel over a part of the -Transcontinental, and I wish to say that I took great delight in reading a folder issued jointly by the Minister of Railways, through the' officials of his department, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, The terms in which they speak of the Transcontinental and the magnificent country through which it passes-a country of splendid resources-was exceedingly gratifying to me.
Mr. REID1: You are not objecting to that.

No. I am glad to see the truth brought out 'by this Government, even though it may falsify the declarations, which its supporters have made from time to time for partisan purposes. Let me read what the Government say of this Transcontinental, -a road which the present right hon. leader of the Opposition said, when he made his plans for its construction, was to roll back the map of Canada, and open -a new empire in this Dominion of our-s. This is wh-at the folder says:
Three railways are combining to make the passenger service over this new route the equal of that offered anywhere on this continent. The finest equipment is being used in the service from its very inception, while the smooth, straight and level roadbed embodies all that

has been learnt in three-quarters of a century by those who build our railways. The greatest comfort is therefore assured both by day and night.
What better testimony could you have of the excellence of the Transcontinental than is afforded by this folder, and afforded truthfully, as I can say, because I have travelled over many of the 'best railroads of the United States, and have never travelled upon a line of railway where *there was more comfort than upon the Transcontinental.
That speaks well for the operation.

It sipeake well for the engineers who built the road under the auspices of the late Government, and it speaks well for the present Department of Railways and Canals for supplying such splendid equipment upon the road between 'Cochrane and Winnipeg. I can only wish that they had extended the same treatment as far -east as Moncton, and given the people of eastern Canada something like the service they aTe giving between Cochrane and Winnipeg.
They will have that very soon.

I hope so. The folder goes on:
" The National " is the name which has been chosen for the principal train in the service on both its east and westbound journeys. It will operate between Toronto and Winnipeg over the lines of the Canadian Government, the Grand Trunk and the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railways, known as " the Transcontinental Line," providing accommodation that will meet the demands of the most exacting.
Then the folder goes on to describe the country traversed by the railway,' a country that hon. gentlemen opposite said would be worthless and never pay for the operation of the road, but in which the Liberal party had such supreme faith that they inaugurated this great undertaking:
At New Liskeard the famous clay belt begins providing a soil for the agriculturist which has few equals. As is the case throughout vast stretches of Northern Ontario the land has been sheltered for ages by the forests. The mould can be measured by feet and underneath is the clay loam. On these lands, in the future, scores of thousands of settlers will make their homes. Englehart is a divisional point, and further on is Sesekinika, with its islands, beautiful playground possibilities, and entry is made into the height of land country. Here the waters divide, heading southward for Lake Timiskaming, the .Ottawa river and the sea, and northward, by way of innumerable lakes to James bay. At Monteith is an interesting experimental farm,
and at Iroquois falls a branch line runs to the world-famous Porcupine gold fields. I
Cochrane is the junction point with the Transcontinental railway, being in the centre of a fertile agricultural country, and is an up-to-date town with a population of 3,000 people.
Much agricultural development in certain sections has already taken place in the territory west of Cochrane to Grant station; this is more especially noticed in the vicinity of Hearst, where a thriving town has sprung up, and it is here that the junction with the Algoma Central railway for Sault St. Marie is made.
The real extent and richnes of Ontario can be realized. The province, three, and one-third times the size of Great Britain and Ireland, is divided into two great sections. The new, or Northern Ontario, through which we are passing is much larger than the older section, covering an area of 350,000 square miles. It is estimated that there are twenty million acres of fertile land awaiting the strong arm of the settler in this region, to say nothing of the natural resources in the form of timber, minerals, game and scenery. There are hundreds of square miles of spruce and poplar lying in easy proximity to great water-powers capable of providing the hydraulic and electric energy necessary to convert the pulpwood into pulp and paper. Splendid crops of grain, hay and potatoes are already being produced.
It goes on to speak of the water-power and of the other wonderful possibilities of that country, making it plain that it was one of the grandest conceptions which public .men could hope to realize that entered into the minds of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), then the leader of the Government, and his colleagues, when they conceived the idea of this new Transcontinental railway. This folder proceeds to say, and to say truthfully:
Wherever this new railway reaches, it opens a new empire, providing homes for the workers of the earth where they may plant and reap abundantly.
And it has the same story to tell when it comes to deal with the millions of acres of land available for settlement as the line crosses the prairie and before it reaches the mountains.
I bring this before the House in the hope that we may hear no more frqm public men in disparagement of the Transcontinental railway. Let us have confidence in that road. I-t is a magnificent undertaking, and if properly managed will develop a country of enormous possibilities, where, in the not distant future, will be found the comfortable homes of hundreds of thousands of people. I have faith in the paying qualities of the Transcontinental railway. But let the Minister of Railways not treat the several sections merely as local roads, but let him, by operation, link up all parts of the system, from the ports on the Atlantic and the grand old city of Quebec to the

cities of the western prairies, and the great province of British Columbia. Let these sections he operated as a transcontinental system;' encourage travel; encourage freight traffic. Operated in the progressive way I have suggested, it will not be long before the earnings of this road will be great and satisfactory. Let me again beg of the acting minister, who has charge of the department: Do not allow the general manager, Mr. Gutelius, to impress upon you the idea that this road is to be operated as part of the Government railway system. That is what Mr. Gutelius has in his mind; that is what he wants to work out; that is what be aims at when he links up MoGivney Junction with the city of Fredericton to connect with the Valley road. That is what he is trying to work out when he is making the Valley road merely a local road and an adjunct of the Canadian Pacific. What we want is to treat the Transcontinental road as a system by itself. We want,, in the very near future, to double track the Intercolonial from Moncton to Halifax, for there will be an enormous trade brought over the Transcontinental if it is operated in a progressive manner. And let there be a direct, short connection between the Transcontinental and the port of St. John. A few years ago, when Mir. Hays was president of the Grand Trunk, and before the late Government went out of power, plans were inaugurated on a large iscale for making great terminal facilities at Quebec, at Halifax, and also at the port of St. John. It provided that immense developments should be made at Courtenay bay, where a new harbour was to be created. Plans were prepared, with the approval of the Grand Trunk Pacific, for that harbour, and it was expected that this would be one of the termini of that system. That is being destroyed, as I have said, by this. Government and their associates in New Brunswick. This Government had legislation passed in 1912 authorizing them to give aid to the bridges, and under that legislation the people of New Brunswick were encouraged to take upon themselves these burdens, amounting to $6,000,000, a staggering obligation for a people of 350,000. Let me say, as one of the representatives of the province of New Brunswick, that we not only ask but demand that this Government should carry out the pledge which by statute enacted by this Parliament it solemnly made to the people of New Brunswick.
I	have felt it to he my duty to speak in this way in the presence of the Acting Minister of Railways, because things are going on in New Brunswick to-day under the guiding hand of Mr. Gutelius, Manager of Government Railways, which cause the people of that province to believe that the Government and not the Grand Trunk Pacific is to manage the Transcontinental road in the future, and that this whole idea of the Valley road from St. John to Grand Falls to be operated as part of the Transcontinental is to be abandoned; that the promise of the Government to build the bridges is to be done away with, and that the road, instead of being built from Grand Falls to St. John, to be operated as part of the Transcontinental, is to be built from Centreville, a small village in Carleton county to Westfield, a small village on the Canadian Pacific, and that instead of being a part of the Transcontinental system it is to become merely an adjunct to the Canadian Pacific railway. of this line as one Transcontinental system by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, which owns the line from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean. The people look to this Government, with a confidence mingled with a certain amount of despair, to take the matter up, even at this late date, and to see that the grave injustice which is threatening the province of New Brunswick may be averted.

I think we all agree that the Transcontinental, now that it has been com. pleted through to Moncton, should be operated in the best interests of the people of Canada. I can assure the hon. members that everything will be done to get all the freight possible, both east and west, over this Transcontinental railway from Halifax to Winnipeg. When we took over this road passenger trains were started between Toronto and Winnipeg, and in a short time we expect to have through trains between Halifax and Winnipeg. I do
11 p.m. not think, therefore, that there is much difference of opinion between members on this side and members on the other side on this question. I do not think that at the next session of Parliament the hon. gentleman will make the complaints that he is making now.	[DOT]

Not on the main line.
The Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific railway, and other railways are expending sums for similar purposes.
Is this an extension? The acting .minister knows that this is not an extension.
Original construction, I say. These railways have further construction every year. With the Transcontinental, as with other railways, there will be construction, I suppose, for very many years.

There will be construction of branches; there will be extensions, improvements and that sort of thing. But the acting minister cannot get away from the fact that this is for original construction of the railway. It is not completed yet, 'and the acting minister knows that it is not.

I have no doubt that the hon. member, if he were in the House, would move to strike out those items, as he comes from the Maritime Provinces and knows the local conditions quite well. He could suggest what paring down ought to be made in the present crisis in the country's interest. I would say a word of Courtenay bay. I visited the spot myself, and I t'hink the previous Government had launched quite a scheme in connection with that work.
A channel a mile long is being dredged out where there is no water at low tide. Likely it was the late minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsiley) who undertook to dig that channel. If you get to Courtenay Bay at low tide, you will find that there is no water and that an artificial channel for ocean steamers is being dredged to a depth of 35 feet. Moreover, a breakwater has to be built at an expenditure of millions and millions as a protection for vessels to prevent their being pushed ashore by the winds. Those contracts entered into at the request of my hon. friend the former Minister of Public Works are not in the country's best interest, but we must of course see them through, since millions have already been expended in the work; millions uselessly wasted, as there is a natural harbour at St. John. The hon. gentleman had enough influence to pass estimates of that magnitude for a mud channel. I hold he should explain his action in that connection before trying to dig out scandals where there is more to be found.
